This must parallel it.
Mi'. DYMENT. The rails have all been taken off some years ago and the road has been abandoned.
Are we to understand that these two miles referred to in this resolution have already been constructed ?
Yes, finished this spring.

Are we to understand that the policy of the government is to allow a company to survey and construct a line of railway, and after it has been constructed for two years to come forward and secure a subsidy from this government for that line of railway ?

I think, there have been cases where railways have been subsidized after the time of their completion. Sometimes there have been understandings in advance that the road would be aided and I think there have been cases where a subsidy has been granted after the completion of a section of road.
Has there been an application before the government during the last two years for the subsidy which we are now voting ?
Yes.
Why was it left for two years ?
Last year there were no subsidies.
On a previous occasion the application was for the whole of this road.
In 1901 we subsidized twenty-one miles of this road.

When this reorganized company took hold of the mines they applied for assistance to build this railway. They were granted nine miles at first, which was afterwards increased to 21, and perhaps part of this is a revote.
Mi-. FOWLER. If it is a revote, it should not appear here.
It is in addition to the previous grant.
This two miles is the total length of the road.
Oli, no ; it is an extension of the 19 miles.

1 understand that the province of Ontario has already subsidized this road, and it is important in every case that we should be informed as to what subsidy has been granted by a province. It may be that the province thought that their subsidy was sufficient to promote the construction of this road. We hear a great deal at present about provincial rights, and it may be that the province of Ontario would be jealous of our subsidizing a road which they have already aided. Can the Finance Minister tell me what subsidy was granted by the province ?
The application of the company says they have received a provincial subsidy for 17 miles, but it does not state the amount.

We certainly should know what subsidy has been granted by the provincial government in every case. If the province gave a large subsidy in land and cash, it does not strengthen their claim to come here and ask for a further subsidy. There is a limit to the extent to which we can aid even deserving schemes, and we might be disposed to take into account the subsidy granted by a province when we are giving aid. We should not proceed in utter disregard of the fact as to whether the province has granted a subsidy or not.
There was no land grant given by the province. It was a subsidy of $3,000 per mile in cash for 17 miles.
For the same road as we are asked to subsidize here ?
No, for about 11 miles of it.

We are groping in the dark. We are granting a subsidy to a road, 17 miles of which has been built, and built with the aid of a provincial subsidy. Why should we, in addition to the ample provision which has been made by the province of Ontario, grant another subsidy for a road that has been already constructed ? The government should see that we are not throwing away the people's money on enterprises that are already provided for by the provincial legislature. I would feel very much disposed to move that this item be not agreed to. I shall investigate it further, because I now think that it is one of those subsidies which should not receive the sanction of this committee.

I am afraid we are a little mixed with regard to this. Some years ago the company made an application for a subsidy and nine miles were subsidized. They built the road and made the property a success. Last year no subsidies were granted, but they went ahead and nearly completed 17 miles, and

the total subsidy will be for 30 miles of road through that important section of the country. They have established their works successfully, and are now carrying the products of other mines as well as of their own. This application has been pressed very strongly and very energetically by the citizens of the district. It is not as if the road were built by a company without any application on their part, or without any reason for them to believe that if they went on and spent their own money and developed the country and established their enterprise, they would not receive assistance. I believe that a great development has taken place in that part of the country because of the little assistance we gave in the past, and which we are now supplementing, by aiding in the construction of this 30 miles of road.

Is this two miles from Bruce Mines to Bruce Mines Junction between the same two points that the Canadian Pacific Railway formerly had a branch ?
Mr. DYMEiNT. Yes.
Are they utilizing the old road ?
No.
Was there a subsidy granted to the Canadian Pacific Railway for that ?

I don't think so. The two miles built by the Canadian Pacific Railway were merely for their own convenience, the same as they would run a line into a gra\ el pit. The Minister of Public Works is quite right in saying that these people were led to believe that if they went on with the work they could look for favourable consideration. The people' insisted that the railway company should build into the town of Bruce Mines, feeling perfectly satisfied that the government would supplement what they had already done, and I think every hon. member will agree that this was much better than that the road should have stopped half way.
They are building on the old road of the Canadian pacific Railway ?
No ; they have taken another route altogether.

A remark was made a moment ago by the hon. member for Hal-ton (Mr. Henderson) to which I would like to refer. He appeared to think that it would be an extraordinary thing for this parliament to supplement a subsidy given by a provincial legislature. Ever since I have had any knowledge of the Department of Railways, and prior thereto, from the time subsidies were first given, it has been customary for the Dominion government to give a subsidy to a meritorious undertaking which had been given or been promised aid by the provin-

cial government. The very fact that the provincial government had aided a railway very much improved its chances of receiving Dominion assistance. One of the things which the government have required at the hands of each company has been that it should satisfy them of its ability to construct the line ; for we know that a subsidy of $3,200 a mile does not at all furnish sufficient means for that purpose. For this particular road I should say that it would be quite inadequate. My information with regard to this road is that it is a much more extensive one than the ordinary railways which we aid, that it passes through a rough and irregular country, and that it will require a good deal of heavy work in its construction. The object which the government have had in view in requiring each company to advise them whether any subsidy had already been given or promised by the provincial government, was not to furnish a ground for objection to the Dominion giving aid. but to justify the application, and to assure the government that if they granted aid, the undertaking would probably be carried through. The information which the acting minister has furnished is as full information as we have ever required from a railway company. With reference to these two miles which have been referred to, I may say that what has been stated by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Dyment) is quite correct, that the company had good reason to expect if they went on with their undertaking and completed these two miles, the government, when considering the subject of giving subsidies at any futur'e time, would give this subject as favourable consideration as they felt they could, and the few days gained. I think, ought not to be any reason why this assistance should not be given.
I am not aware that any person on this side of the House made any objection to a grant being made to any particular railway on account of its having received aid from the provincial government.
I so understood the hon. member for Halton.

I thought the exminister was directing his attention to me ; because I am of the same opinion as he, that unless the combined subsidies would be largely in excess of the requirements for the purpose of building the road, we could have no better evidence of faith in the scheme than the fact that it had received aid from the provincial government. I never heard any objection raised on that ground. Nor have I any objection to a subsidy having an ex post facto effect; because if the parties have gone on in good faith and built a road which tends to the development of the country, I think they are as much entitled to the money as if the undertaking were in prospect.

I fear that I did not make myself plain to the ex-Minister of Railways. What I intended to elicit by asking whether this road had received a provincial subsidy or not was such information as would warrant us in granting the vote asked for. We are asked to vote $3,200 a mile to assist this enterprise ; but that may be increased to $6,400 a mile, depending altogether on the cost of the construction of the road. We might consider that a fair subsidy ; and to my mind it should be quite sufficient for the construction of a road into that country, which is referred to by the promoters as one which will produce an enormous amount of traffic, a comparatively rich section, especially in timber and in mines. If that is the. case, and the road has already received a subsidy of $3,000 per mile from the local legislature, the combined subsidies will amount to $9,400 per mile, which seems to me to be a very large subsidy for a road into that section. Under these circumstances, I think we ought to be informed whether or not some provision has already been made for the construction of this road. If so, possibly it would be wise on our part not to grant the full subsidy given to roads aided by the province, but to limit the amount and bring it within reason. I rather approve of the policy laid down last night by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock), who suggested that we should have the fullest information, and that all these matters should be referred to the transportation commission for full and ample reports regarding them. At any rate, we should be put in possession of information as to the probable cost of these roads and the character and value of the country through which they run, so that we could vote intelligently on these matters. While I do not consider the fact of a provincial bonus having been granted an oo-jection to our granting aid in a meritorious case, a knowledge of how much the province has given would enable us to decide on what we should do here. Therefore in every case \Ve should be put in possession of these facts.

Let me point out to my hon. friend that before this road could receive the subsidy of $6,400 per mile, it would have to cost $21,400 per mile. If it were to receive $6,400 from the Dominion and $3,000 from the province, it would then have $9,400 for a road costing upwards of $21,000 per mile.
Don't you think that is a pretty good bonus ?

A good deal would depend on the conditions. There are portions of the country where you could not get a road built with that. At the same time, I agree with my hon. friend that it is always desirable to know what the province contributes. Having regard to the conditions of the country through which

this railway is to run. I do not think the promoters, even if they get all the subsidies which my hon. friend mentions, will make very much out of it.
Might I ask the hon. member for Algoma if the subsidy from the Ontario government has already been paid to the company ?
I cannot tell the hon. gentleman that.
I noticed, when the hon. member from Algoma made the statement that this road had already been constructed and was completed almost two years ago, the acting Minister of Railways seemed surprised.
This part, which is only a portion of the whole line, was finished last spring.
I said that we had subsidized twenty-one miles, and have paid a subsidy on nine miles as completed. I did not make any statement with regard to these two particular miles.
But the hon. gentleman understood why this subsidy was applied for, the two miles had not been completed.
I was not clear on that point.

It is evident that when these people applied for a subsidy, they held back from the government the most important information. The fact is the hon. Minister of Finance asked the committee to vote a subsidy when he had not the information as to whether this road was completed or not. I think it is a wrong policy for any government to allow any set of contractors to go on constructing a portion of road, whether two miles or twenty miles, and then, after it is constructed, seek and obtain a subsidy. When promoters require a subsidy, they should ask for it before beginning the road.

I am not quite clear about the extent of this road. I understood the acting Minister of Railways to say that the first subsidy in 1901 was for twenty-one miles, and if this is also for twenty-one miles, that would make forty-two miles.

Only nine miles were subsidized two years ago, which, with these twenty-one miles, makes a total of thirty miles.
To the James Bay Railway Company for a line of railway from Toronto, via the east side of Lake Simeoe, Parry Sound, and Sudbury, towards James Bay, not exceeding 265 miles, in lieu of two subsidies granted by chapter S of 1900. of 35 and 20 miles respectively, from Parry Sound towards James Bay.
Might I ask an explanation of this particular subsidy ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: This was the subject of some reference last evening. It will connect the city of Toronto with the northern portion of Ontario. Several deputations waited on the government urging that this line should be subsidized.
Is it intended to be a connection of the Canadian Pacific Railway from Toronto to Sudbury ?
It will cross the Canadian Pacific Railway at Sudbury, and connect ultimately with the new transcontinental.
Who constitute the James Bay Railway Company ?
Mackenzie & Mann.
This runs half a mile from the Northern Railway at many points.
The Northern Railway runs west of Lake Simeoe, while this runs east of Lake-Simeoe.
Has this company a Dominion or a provincial charter ?
A Dominion charter.
What is the length of the road ?

I have forgotten. This charter has been in existence some years, and the first real work was commenced two or three years ago, when they started to build north from Parry Sound on the subsidy now being revoted. The total mileage now being subsidized is 265 miles. I think this is perhaps the most important subsidy we are asked to grant. It will bring the whole western section of northern Ontario into direct communication not only- with the Canadian Pacific Railway, but with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and will afford a through route to the west. Moreover, it will develop a splendid country' north from Parry Sound. Of course, close to Toronto, there is already railway' communication, but this, which is really a transcontinental line, will do more to benefit western Ontario-than any other scheme dealt with in these subsidy resolutions.
Is this road intended togo on to James Bay ?
Yes.

It should be pushed through there then ; that is a great country.
To the Quebec and Lake- St. John Railway-Company for one mile of railway from Roberval to the government wharf at Lake St. John.
Is there any' explanation of this ?

I tliouglit tlie modesty of this item would so commend it that it would be at once approved. The object is to carry the present terminus of the Quebec and Lake St. John Railway to the wharf at Roberval, that is about a mile.

At least, a scheme of this kind does not call for ' mountains of information ' to convince the House of the propriety of it. But it seems strange to apply for a subsidy to build a road to a government wharf. Anyhow it seems a very small matter to trouble the government with. Of course, the information is very meagre, but I apprehend that it would be cheaper to allow the item to pass than to occupy the time of the House in discussing it.
To the Interprovineial and James Bay Railway Company on a line of railway from Lake Timis-kaming at the present terminus of the Canadian Pacific Railway line, in a northerly direction. not to exceed 50 miles.
Is that the same company as the one to which the subsidy has been given for 265 miles ?

This is a company to build an extension of a railway that now runs from Mattawa northward in the direction of Lake Timiskaming, on the Quebec side. It is proposed to build a road to the village of Yille Marie. As everybody knows, this is an excellent agricultural country, which is rapidly being colonized and developed.
This is simply an extension from the end of the Canadian Pacific Railway line. What is this ?
The incorporators are mostly gentlemen in Ottawa and in the locality of Timiskaming.
Is this a different company from the James Bay Railway Company ?
Absolutely.

Would it not be better to offer this subsidy to a line of railway from Lake Timiskaming, running in a northern direction fifty miles, instead of confining it to this Interprovincial and James Bay Company ? The only possible way to get the extension of the line is to induce the Canadian Pacific Railway to extend their line which now runs from Mattawa up along the shore of the Lake Timiskaming. To put it in the form I suggest, gives the government the opportunity to make arrangements, and not give a special status to parties who are mere intermediaries between the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway.

The company applied for the subsidy. We inquired about them, and as the company is one of
thorough respectability, I see no reasons why we should not grant the subsidy.
The respectability of the company is not in question. But the fact is that this piece of route will be absolutely of no use unless the company make some arrangement with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I dare say.

Then, as suggested by my bon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart), it ought to be left an open question. I care not what the respectability of the company may be, they should not be made the intermediary between the government and the railway company that will actually build the line. The question is simply how the country is to be served, and not what is to be the position of the Canadian Pacific Railway or of the promoters, of this scheme. I think the proposition of the hon. member for South Lanark is a very fair one.

I do not see that it is fair. It did not strike us so at alt events. The company made an application, and I am sure that the considerations which now present themselves did not occur to us. We wished to see the road built, and, it seemed apparent that the company would build it.
But the company will be unable to do anything unless they make arrangements with the other company to complete the road.
Then, they will have to make the arrangements.

But we should make provisions designed to secure the building of this road for the people, and not depend upon any haphazard arrangement. It is not unreasonable, in a case like this, to ask that the subsidy be given to a line of railway rather than to a particular company,

The Canadian Pacific Railway were approached times without number asking for this extension of their road from Kippewa lake, or the foot of Lake Timiskaming-Timiskaming station, as they call it-northward.	That road was built
some years ago and the extension has been greatly needed, but the people were unable to get any satisfactory assurance from the Canadian Pacific Railway that the road would be built. Men living in Yille Marie,, who have been settled there for the last twenty years, went to the trouble of organizing a company, and these men are the promoters of the Interprovincial and James Bay road. They are all men of substance, and I think it would be most unfair if, after they have gone to all this trouble, they should be cut out. I do not think the Canadian Pacific Railway are opposed to it at all. The Canadian Pacific Railway were in
l

sympathy with their application in the first place, and said : We are not prepared to go on, but you go on and get a charter and build a road, and we will help you. I do not think the Canadian Pacific Railway would ask that this subsidy should be changed from the company named to another company not named.	,
On what side of Lake Timiskaming does this road run ?
On the Quebec side. It is opening up a large and important section near the head of Lake Timiskaming. I suppose there are 3,000 or 4,000 people in there at the present time.

We are not questioning the necessity of a road at all, but we want to know who is going to get the benefit of it. The hon. gentleman told us it would be too bad to refuse a grant to these gentlemen who had spent their money. For what purpose ? To make something out of it.
They want to get a road.

Is this an enterprise in which these gentlemen have large vested interests themselves, or is it merely an enterprise that they have set on foot for the purpose of making money out of it ? Who are the parties interested ? I am not defending the rights of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, they have no rights that I know of. It is the public rights I am looking after. Here is a case where it is proposed to put a link at the end of a railway belonging to the Canadian Pacific Railway, extending their line and depending upon the Canadian Pacific Railway to give them an outlet. Now, who are the parties who made the application, and who' are spending the money ?

I cannot give you from memory the names of the parties. I know that one of the promoters is a resident of Ville Marie, Mr. A. E. Guay, a very respectable and responsible citizen of that place, a gentleman worth probably $100,000 or $150,000. I think Sir. Ranger is another.
I accompanied these gentlemen down here on a deputation asking for a subsidy, though I cannot give their names from memory.
I also remember when they got their charter the winter before last, when I attended with them a meeting of the Railway Committee. If the hon. gentleman will refer to the charter he will find the names of the promoters, and they are all men of substance.

When a proposal is made to make a grant to a line of railway without stating any particular company, I do not see any objection, according to the hon. gentleman's own statement, to the proposition made by the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart).

I am satisfied there is not one man interested in this enterprise who Mr. McCOOL.
desires to make a dollar of profit out of it, except as an indirect consequence of this road helping settlers in that section of the country, and benefiting any of the promoters who happen to live there. I cannot understand why the hon. member for Both-well should object to granting this subsidy to a named company, a company who have gone to the trouble of getting their charter, when there is no opposition to it from anybody. There is no opposition by the Canadian Pacific Railway, at least I do not think there is ; and I cannot see any reason why they should not be granted a subsidy under the name of an incorporated company.

I want to say a word of explanation respecting the Bruce Mines and Algoma Railway. I find that my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Dy-ment) was correct, and that the former vote was for nine miles. How the memorandum given to me said 27 miles I cannot explain.
For a line of railway from Waltham station to Ferguson Point in the county of Pontiac not exceeding 20 miles.
This is for an extension westward of the Pontiac and Pacific Junction Railway from its present terminus to Ferguson, on the Ottawa river.

Why is a distinction made in this case ? This is for a line of railway, the other was for a railway company. Who are the promoters of this road ?
Mi-. McCOOL. I think the reason for the distinction is that the Canadian Pacific Railway, who now own the Pontiac and Pacific Junction Railway, would not make application for the subsidy, although I think they are anxious to get the extension. The Pontiac and Pacific Junction Railway hold a charter covering that ground. The road has been built to Waltham for the last ten or twelve years or more. I ought to know a good deal about it, because I was born about half way between the two points on this road. I am quite satisfied that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will make the extension. If they do not, then I think they will make no objection to another company building.
Has not the Canadian Pacific Railway Company got a charter ?
They have got a charter covering this ground.
Ig it not the intention of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to build a bridge across there ?
I presume it is.
It is with the expectation that the Canadian Pacific Railway will really build it.

Is there a bonus to this particular road already from this government ?
14450
No.
There was a bonus.

It has lapsed.
To the Quebec Central Railway Company for an extension of its line of railway from St. Francois to St. George, not exceeding nine miles; also for a railway from Scott junction to the Quebec bridge, not exceeding 22 miles.

This is an extension of the Quebec Central Railway along the valley of the ChaudiSre river. At present the Quebec Central Railway starts from Quebec, or to speak more correctly, from Levis and enters the valley of the Chau-diere river.
It enters the valley of the Etcliemin river first.

No, it does not, it goes- down by the Intercolonial Railway to Harlaka Junction and then goes south into the valley of the ChaudiSre river. This is to extend the present terminus from the valley of the ChaudiSre nine miles to the valley of the St. George. At Scott Junction there is a duplication of the railway. One section goes along the valley of the Chau-difire to St. Francis and the other section crosses the railway and goes to Sherbrooke and the Eastern Townships. This is required in order that there may be a railway built directly to the Quebec'bridge, a distance of twenty-two miles.
There is no railway there now ?
There is a railway going eastward to the Intercolonial Railway near St. Charles. This would cut off all that section, giving a straight line to the Quebec bridge.
This is not built ?
No, it is to be built.

I would like to inform the government that in building this road they are taking one step towards the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific. It was stated in the House some time ago that one reason why they would not build the Grand Trunk Pacific through the county of Dorchester was that it would give a longer route. Let me tell the House that by building this road from the Quebec bridge to Scott Junction you are building a road twenty miles exactly on the line that I have proposed. I may say, further, that in the case yon build the Grand Trunk Pacific here you will by this be killing two birds with the one stone, and in places you will be killing three' birds with one stone. You must remember that the road would be built from St. George, in the county of Beauce. St. George lies exactly west of a parish in the county of Dorchester called Ste. Justine. Ste. Justine is the natural gap, or the place for a railway to go through there. It is a very level piece of farming land. If the government build this Grand Trunk Pacific Railway it will start from the Quebec bridge, and if the government should send the man who is sitting there beside the minister, Mr. Schrieber, in whom I and every person else have the utmost confidence, to that district and tell him to locate a railway line, he will undoubtedly locate it through the places I have mentioned. Then, besides that, if you build a railway where I am asking it, you will serve the demands made by my bon. friend from Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan), who has a charter, as we all know, from River St. Francis to Quebec, and by building this line you run a road exactly where he wants it. Then the Quebec Central Railway Company has a charter from St. George up the valley of the Famine river about eighteen miles to Ste. Justine, from Ste. Justine then to this Lake Pohenagamook you would be running on the same line again, from that lake in the county of Temiscouata there you would serve the Quebec Central, the road asked by my hon. friend from Victoria, N.B., and you would serve the government road. You would need to build only one road where there are three applications for roads, and therefore I say that you would be killing three birds with one stone.
You would not be killing Costigan, though.

Then, from Quebec through to St. Isidore, in Dorchester county, this one road would do for all. The Quebec Central in building from Quebec bridge, will have to go through St. Isidore and then go straight soutli to Scott Junction. If the government builds the road they will have to build in the exact place I am now mentioning. It would be wise for the government before dabbling into all these things to send my friend Mr. Schreiber there and let him look at the country and the location; he will undoubtedly say that I am perfectly right. It makes no difference who says I am wrong; I say I am right and I know it.
Carried.
No, it is not carried.
Surely no further explanation is required after the speech to which we have just listened.

The explanation which has just been given demands a further explanation. The hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin) has stated that if the government carried out their contemplated scheme of a National Transcontinental Railway, it would traverse practically the same territory and serve the same purpose as the road to which it is now proposed to give a subsidy. If that be true-and the hon. gentleman no doubt speaks with very definite information

-it seems to me that that puts an end to any argument that the railway will serve a country that cannot be otherwise served. If the statement be true it is an alarming one,
that when we have passed an Act giving the government power to build a railway over this same territory, to serve the same purpose, that some gentleman makes an application for a subsidy and we grant it, knowing all these facts. Unless there is some explanation following the statement of the hon. member for Dorchester, this committee should make inquiry and have definite information before consenting to this vote.

There are two branches of railway now asked to be subsidized under this item. One is an extension of the existing railway along the Chaudiere valley from St. Francis to St. George, and my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Morin) will say to my hon. friend behind him (Mr. Clancy) that the Transcontinental Railway can have nothing whatever to do with that railway; one goes west whereas the Transcontinental Railway is going east. That settles that point. In regard to the other section of railway from Scott Junction to the Quebec bridge is a distance of twenty-two miles. That is all there is and how far the new railway will parallel this railway, I cannot at present say. That will depend very much on the route to be taken by the new railway. I think that if the railway which is to be built is to follow the Etchemin river it would to some extent parallel this railway. If it does not follow the Etchemin river, after leaving the Quebec bridge, it must go east and would not come in contact with this railway except for a few miles. There are several railways which must in the future come to the Quebec bridge. Already there are the Grand Trunk Railway, the Intercolonial Railway, and probably another road, the South Shore Railway will come to the Quebec bridge. The Transcontinental Railway must leave the Quebec bridge and go south and east and will parallel this for a few miles only.

If you want to build a road from the Quebec bridge south you have to go to the west of St. Jean Chrysostome church and then east of the St. Lambert de L-Svis church, and then right through the parsonage of the St. Isidore church. You cannot help doing this owing to the nature of the country and then from there my hon. friend says the line will follow the valley of the Etchemin river. You must not follow the Etchemin valley at all.
For a transcontinental railway ?
No, Sir. What I am saying is right,, and if Mr. Schreiber and I go on the road, as I have gone with him before. I believe we will agree as to that point. You start from the Quebec bridge, and you go

straight south through the parish of St. Isidore, which is about eighteen miles from the bridge. Then you go two miles beyond that, and then the Grand Trunk Pacific will still follow a straight course south or south-east. Then the road of the Quebec Central, a little beyond St. Isidore, would turn to the right on account of a hill there, and go to Scott junction. You must go through the village in which I live, although the people do not want a road there because it is not necessary. Then you go on through the parishes of Ste. Marguerite, St. Malachie and St. Clair, striking the corners of these four parishes. [DOT] Then you strike the Etchemin river at St Malachie, and you follow the river clear through to the outlet of lake Etchemin, whence you go to St. Germain. Then you go four miles beyond, when you strike the waters of the Famine river which flows into the 'Chaudiere river ; you then turn to the left a few degrees, and you strike the summit of the Chaudiere river and the Etchemin river, and then you go eastward through all the other counties. You will thus serve every county on the south side of the mountains. But if you adopt the line that has been spoken of by my hon. friend from Belleclmsse (Mr. Talbott from the Quebec bridge to the mouth of the Abenakis river, you would only be a nile or a mile and a half apart. After you leave the Quebec bridge, you would commence to ascend the mountains for about fifty miles, until you get probably a thousand feet high. The ascent is not very great from the Quebec bridge until you get to the Abenakis river, but then you strike a very heavy grade for about eight miles until you get to the Pine river, when you turn to your right. If you adopt the route which I have suggested, you follow the natural course of the valley the whole way. As I have already stated in this House, the only two rivers in the province of Quebec which cross the Alleghany Mountains are the Richelieu river and the Etchemin river and we all know that when you have a stream to cut the mountain for you, you are at a great advantage in railway construction.
For the first nine miles we grant a subsidy to the Quebec Central Railway Company, and the subsidy for the other two miles is granted to any railway company.
No.
Well, even suppose it is granted to the Quebec Central Company, what purpose is served by this road, which will not be served by the Trans-continental railway if it is built ?

I do not know that the Transcontinental Railway has auy-thing to do with the present vote. This subsidy here will go to the Quebec Central Railway, and will accommodate three or

lour parishes which have no rail connection now. It will shorten the entrance of the Quebec Central Railway from the United States into Quebec city.

From Scott Junction to Quebec, the Quebec Central will have two roads :	One to Lfivis and one to
the Quebec bridge. It is the intention that the National Transcontinental Railway will take over the present line of the Quebec Central up as far as St. Anselme.
I do not know what will be done with the Transcontinental Railway. At the present it is the intention to give a subsidy to the Quebec Central Railway.
From Scott Junction to the St. Lawrence, the Quebec Central would have two railways.
Yes.

Are we going to lay down the principle that we are to give subsidies to a road paralleling the road of the same company for four or five miles. It may shorten the distance, but it is a mere convenience to the railway company. We must have money very plentiful when we do that.

My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is labouring under a mistake. This is not to make the Quebec Central line any shorter, but instead of going to Levis it enables them to aim for the Quebec bridge. Owing to the construction of the Quebec bridge every road on the south side of the river will want to get to it now. Circumstances alter cases. The Quebec Central cannot handle heavy freight from Levis for about thirty-five miles. From Harlaka Junction they have a very heavy grade, and ten miles further on they strike another almost impossible grade of a mile and a half. Passenger trains find it very difficult to clinch that grade. That prevents them handling heavy freight, but the route which they now propose will avoid all that, and it does not come to the same point as the old road at all. At LSvis the two roads will be probably nine miles apart, and this new road will enable them to handle heavy freight from the north to the south.

As I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Morin), all the roads are now aiming to get to the Quebec bridge, and I can quite understand that. But are we going to start out on the principle of subsidizing all the railways to reach that bridge, instead of subsidizing lines to serve the public in a wider sense ? I may not have grasped the situation properly, but so far as I am able to judge, we are subsidizing a railway now to reach the Quebec bridge, which is hardly in the proper sens? of the word a national undertaking at all :	it is
a private enterprise. Instead of having in view the serving of the public generally, we are subsidizing railways all tending to
that bridge. If my information is correct, this is not justifiable.

The answer which my hon. friend asks for has already been given by my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Morin). He has stated reasons which ought to satisfy my hon. friend that while this new railway goes to the Quebec bridge, it will serve a section of country which is at present devoid of railways, and is entitled to the same help that we give to other sections,
I understood the hon. member for Dorchester to say that the transcontinental railway, if built, will serve the same purpose.
Not at all. It is on a different side of the river.

Might I give a few words of information on this matter ? The Quebec Central Railway, leaving Scott Junction, the terminus of the line which is proposed to be subsidized, runs in a north-easterly direction to Harlaka Junction, which is a station on the Intercolonial Railway, about five miles east of L6vis. The proposed line will run due south from the Quebec bridge to Scott Junction. The Quebec bridge will be the terminus of all these different lines of railway ; but the Grand Trunk Pacific line will run in a south-easterly direction, while the proposed line will run due south, along the valley of the Chaudiere river. The Et-chemin river flows into the St. Lawrence about three miles east of the Chaudiere river and takes a south-easterly course, and that is the course which the Grand Trunk Pacific will eventually take in that part of the country. The hon. member for Dorchester knows very well that if the Grand Trunk Pacific were to follow the Chaudiere river through the parishes lie has named to Scott Junction, it would have to run in a southerly direction. The hon. gentleman said a moment ago that the two railways would follow a similar route. My hon. friend knows very well that if the Grand Trunk Pacific were to follow that direction, it would have to be forced out of its course to take a southerly direction, to follow the valley of the Chaudiere river, instead of following the valley of the Etchemin river, and then striking eastward through Belle-chasse, Montmagany, and so on. If it followed the course my hon. friend suggests, it would be forced to go to Lake Etchemin and then on to the boundary line and through the state of Maine.

Before this is carried, I wish to draw the attention of the committee to the way in which this matter has come before the government. I think it] has been brought to the attention of the government in a way that we cannot entirely approve of. The only application 1 made was for a portion of the subsidy, and that comes from the hon. member for Beauce

(Mr. Belaud). He applied for a subsidy for the Quebec Central Railway from St. Francois to St. George, a distance of nine miles, and stated that the district to be served by the extension was very large, comprising nine towns, with no water communication and no railway communication whatever, and that a population of 10,000 people would be immediately and directly benefited by the extension. This recommendation applied entirely to the nine miles. We have no reference whatever to the twenty-two miles. I wonder who made the application for the subsidy for that portion. There seems to be something in the dark, something hidden. The impression of lion, members on this side is that this subsidy for the twenty-two miles is for some secret purpose, and the government so far has not disclosed who is to benefit by it. Is it recommended by anybody at all, or is it to assist a road for which a charter has been obtained by some other hon. member of this House who does not desire his name to come before the committee ? X think we are entitled to more information with respect to these twenty-two miles, because the manner in which the application has come before the government and the committee indicates that there is something kept baek which ought to be disclosed.

The line of the Quebec Central Railway extends from the city of Sherbrooke up the valley of the ChaudiSre river, crosses the river, runs through Dorchester and on to Harlaka Junction. If my hon. friend will look at the map, he will see that this road, once it leaves the ChaudiSre river, runs north and easterly. The intention is to extend the railway from Scott Junction, the point' on the ChaudiSre river where it starts to run in an easterly direction, beginning in Beauce, passing through Dorchester and on into Levis, and ending at the Quebec bridge. It seems desirable to extend this road for the purpose of its business from Scott Junction to the bridge, because at the present time to reach the bridge it describes the two sides of a triangle, one of the sides being the Intercolonial Railway ; and recently the Minister of Railways had the pleasure of listening to a complaint which the manager of the Quebec Central Railway made of excessive charges on the part of the Intercolonial. It is to avoid the necessity of using the Intercolonial from Harlaka Junction to Levis that this extension is asked for. I do not know how the application came to be made, but there were certainly several interviews in which the general manager^and traffic manager applied for this extension. With respect to the nine miles, that is at the other end of the Quebec Central. At present it runs from Beauce Junction to St. Francois, from which point the intention is to extend it to St. George. The valley of the ChaudiSre, which will be served by this extension, is probably one of the most fertile portions of Mr. HENDERSON.
the whole province of Quebec. Last season ten million pounds of butter and cheese were taken out of that valley and four million pounds of maple sugar by this Quebec Central Railway, but owing to the lack of facilities to reach Quebec, these goods had to be sent to Montreal for export. This will all be remedied when this line is extended down to the bridge. It will cross the bridge to the harbour at Quebec and the freight will be deposited alongside the steamers.
The hon. gentleman has not told us who applied for this subsidy.

Mr. Grundy, the general manager of the company, and Mr. Walsh, the assistant traffic manager, both in my presence, applied for it, but I could not say whether any formal application was made in writing.
Is there a charter for the road from Scott Junction to the bridge ?
Yes.
Is it a good farming country V

Yes.
For a line ot railway from the station of Lac Bouchette on the Quebec and Lake St. John Railway to St. AndrS, not exceeding 13 miles.

This is a line from the present line in the valley of the Lake St. John from a station called Lac Bouchette, on the present line in the valley of the Lake St. John extending to a new parish where there is a large pulp establishment and other industries.

I was rather amused at the reasons advanced by the gentleman who applied for this subsidy. He says that the government has already subsidized lines of less importance than ours, and hopes that they will give personal attention to the matter. To my mind that is a very poor reason indeed.
For a line of railway from Quebec towards Seven Islands, including branches to Murray Bay and Bale St. Paul, not exceeding 200 miles.

Seven Islands is on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, opposite the western end of the Island of Anticosti. The intention is to build from Quebec to Seven Islands. Whether or not that is possible is a question for the engineers. A great deal of work has been done at Seven Islands by the capitalists interested in this project, and they are under the impression that the line is feasible. While the whole of the north shore of the St. Lawrence looks from the river like a sea of mountains, it appears that behind these mountains there is a level valley through which a road can be built. The intention is to build branches from the main line to Baie St. Paul, and also to Murray

Bay, which is a very important point, j especially during the summer season.
I should he glad if the hon. Minister of Justice who, no doubt, is familiar with this section of country, would tell us the probable cost of the road ?

I am speaking absolutely without any accurate information. But the preliminary surveys or, I should say, the explorations that have been made from the Bay of Seven Islands up towards Chicoutimi would indicate that the expenditure would be in the neighbourhood of $30,000 per mile. As to the road from Chicoutimi to Quebec, I cannot say anything, except that the country through which the road will run is in some respects similar to the country through which the Lake St. John Railway runs. And I understand that that road cost $20,000 or $25,000 a mile.

I understand that this is a very mountainous country, and that is one of the reasons why the company applied for a larger subsidy than is asked for by any other company. Their application is for a minimum subsidy of $6,400 a mile.
That is not granted.

The reasons given why that subsidy should be greater than to other companies are that it is to pass through a mountainous country and that the country is almost wholly uninhabited. What object can there be in granting a subsidy of $6,400 a mile for a railway into a mountainous country almost uninhabited ?
No, no.
That is what the applicants say.
That may be from Chicoutimi east, but not from Chicoutimi west.

The reasons given for granting a subsidy are as follows : Mountainous country, almost wholly uninhabited; open up extensive agricultural, timber and mining areas ; will cost in excess of $25,000 a mile ; and make Bay of Seven Islands a great national port. Now. I am not sure that it is desirable that we should commence. at this hour, to open up any more national ports. Our ports at Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax require a good deal of money to equip them, and I fail to see that there could be any great advantage in encouraging this enterprise, if one of the most important objects is to establish a national port at the Bay of Seven Islands. However. I think we can console ourselves with the thought that there is very little danger of the subsidy ever being called for.
For a branch line from a point on the Canadian Pacific Railway at or near St. Philippe d'Argenteuil. thence in a northerly direction,
passing through the village of Brownsburg, not exceeding three miles.

This description is not very accurate, so I move that the resolution he amended to read :
For a branch lino from a point at or near the intersection of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Great Northern Railway between St. Phillippe d'Argenteuil and Lacbute, thence in a northerly direction passing through the village of Brownsburg a distance not exceeding three miles.
Mr. HUGHES (Victoria!. Is this in order to run to the cartridge factory ?
The main industries to be accommodated are the factory at Browns-burg and a very extensive quarry beyond that village.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: This is another of the class of applications tliat come before this House in very objectionable form. I do not think that it is in keeping with the dignity of this House that one member of tlie government should write to another member of the government asking for a subsidy for a railway in which' he or his friends may be interested. It would be much better if the application came from some other source. The only application I find for a subsidy for this road is a letter from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Pr&fontaine) addressed to Hon. Mr. Fielding, acting Minister of Railways. That looks very much like a family compact concern. I wonder who owns the granite quarry that this road is to reach, for which we are to give a subsidy of about $10,000.

I bad much pleasure in supporting this application for a subsidy. I was approached on the subject by the president of the Dominion Cartridge Factory, which company, as the committee are aware, has extensive works at Brownsburg. This road will be of great benefit to that industry, as well as to the quarry already mentioned. So far as the quarry is concerned, the supply is unlimited, the only difficulty in the way of developing the quarry being tbe transportation difficulties the company have been obliged to contend witli. The company already employ seventy hands, and I am informed that the amount of their pay-roll is #5.000 a month. In these figures I am speaking from memory, but I think they are accurate. I am also informed that if this road is built the amount of business will probably lie quadrupled : in fact, that there is no limit to the amount of business which can be done, if the transportation difficulty is overcome. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson), who asked the question, will do me the honour of a visit at my home. I shall have great pleasure in driving him, not only to the Cartridge Company's works, but to the quarry. I will make his visit as pleasant for him as possible, and when he has seen what is

going on there I think he will agree that this subsidy will result in benefit to the country.

I thank the hon. gentleman (Mr. Christie) for his invitation, which I gladly accept. I am informed by some of my friends who have visited him that he is a very hospitable entertainer, and so 1 shall be glad, as soon as I can make it convenient, to go down and spend a day with him. He has told us that this quarry is a very valuable one, that the supply is almost inexhaustible, that they employ so many men and pay so much money-in fact he has told us almost everything that we had not inquired about. We on this side were interested in knowing who were the owners of this quarry. I am not so much interested in knowing the great value of the property. I have no doubt it is valuable, otherwise they would not ask the government to subsidize a road leading to it.
How many miles ?
Three miles.

The president of the company is Mr. Brunet, not the gentleman of that name who was formerly a member of this House.
Mr. MARCH, (Bonaventure). He is a large stone and marble dealer in the city of Montreal.
Has the cartridge company now any railway communication to this place ?

The nearest point is St. Phillippe. The company have spent large sums of money on this road, but owing to the heavy freight carried over it the road is in constant need of repair. I have several letters from the president of the company and other gentlemen who are anxious to see this branch line constructed.
To the Orford Mountain Railway Company for a line of railway from a point on its main line between Lawrenceville and Eastman to Lake Bonella, five miles; from Kingsbury to Windsor Mills, ten miles; and from Eastman to the town line between township of Bolton, east part, and township of Potton, 12 miles, not exceeding in the whole 27 miles.
This is a small road in the eastern townships under a Quebec charter.
Did this company get their charter amended here, and obtain a Dominion charter ?
I do not think so.

I think this was a Quebec charter that had very extensive privileges, and the promoters came to this House and endeavoured to get a Bill passed with all these privileges granted by the Quebec charter, and they failed. I would like to know how much of it is built ?

This road happens to be in my neighbourhood, and I am well acquainted with the circumstances. It is a small road in the eastern townships, constructed by the Orford Mountain Railway Company, composed of local men entirely. It starts at present from the village of Eastman and runs northward to a place called Kingsbury. They are now seeking to build a branch line from a point between Lawrenceville and Eastman on their main line to Lake Bonella, where there are large lumbering operations carried on, and they wish to extend it from Kingsbury to Windsor Mills, on the main line of the Grand Trunk, between Montreal and Portland. They also wish to extend their line southwards from the village of Eastman, about six miles, in the hope of carrying it further at some future time to touch the International boundary line, where they can connect with American lines.
Was not a part of this road abandoned once V

No. not under the name of the Orford Mountain Railway. There was a railway company called the Missisquoi and Black River Valley Railway Company, that is now defunct. They built a few miles, but the rails have been taken up and the road has been abandoned. The Orford Mountain Railway desires to construct the portion from Eastman southwards partly on the old embankment of that road. But practically it is a new' construction entirely.
To the Atlantic. Quebec and Western Railway Company for a line of railway from GaspS to a point at or near Causapscal on the Intercolonial Railway, and from that point to Edmundston, N.B.. not exceeding 260 miles ; and for a line of railway from Paspebiac to GaspS as near the shore as practicable, not exceeding 102 miles. Total, 362 miles.

As the House is aware, this charter was granted at the beginning of this session. The road starts from Paspebiac, in the county of Bonaventure, and will run along the shore as far as Gaspe Basin. Thence the road will go into the interior of the peninsula and reach Causapscal, on the Intercolonial, and from there will go as [DOT] far as Edmundston, in New Brunswick, where it will tap the American system. On the shores of the Baie des Chaleurs from Paspebiac to Gaspf; bay, there are from 20,000 to 25,000 people, who have hitherto been deprived of railway communication. This company has agreed to build that line at the urgent request of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Mareil), and at my own request. They intended at first to build a railway only into the interior of the peninsula, where they have large interests. I may say at once that the Gasp6 coast is a very fine agricultural country, and the interior of the peninsula is very rich in natural resources of all kinds. To show the

bona tides of the company, I may say that before they procured this charter-because they were incorporated under a local charter- they made all the preliminary surveys, and diming last winter they expended a least .$60,000 or $75,000. I will read to the Committee a letter which I have just received from the manager of the road, Mr. Carpenter. Some gentlemen from London, England, are interested in this construction. Mr. Carpenter writes as follows :
Montreal, October 16, 1903. Dear Sir.-Now that our company has been assured they will receive a cash subsidy from the Dominion government, the directors feel justified in instructing their engineers to push forward the work with all despatch. Our engineer in chief is Mr. Henry O'Sullivan-
Who is well known to some lion, gentlemen in this House.
-who informed me last week that the preliminary or location survey was quite complete, and the draughtsman would have the plans and reports of the same from the Intercolonial to Gaspe Basin ready for us in the course of a week or ten days. In the meantime I have instructed Mr. O'Sullivan to get together the necessary staff of engineers, transit men, labourers, &c., ready to proceed to Gaspe and start the final survey for construction. Owing to the lateness of the season we do not contemplate being able to survey and complete the plan of more than three sections of the road before winter sets in. two in the county of Bonaventure and one from Gaspg, in all thirty miles. If we are not prevented by inclement weather we shall have these plans completed and be in a position to start construction on the above sections early next spring.
How many miles?

Thirty miles at present, because, as the hon. gentleman will notice by looking at the report, the company has had imposed upon it very stringent conditions. For instance, the company is obliged to build concurrently the shore line and the interior line, and if the company does not build ten miles within a year, dating from the 21st of June, on which day the Bill was sanctioned by the Governor General in the Senate, their charter will lapse, not only for the shore line, but for the interior line as well.
We will extend it; all you have to do is to come and ask for an extension of time and we w'll grant it to you.
I am glad to receive the endorsation of my hon. friend and his promise of an extension. I thank my hon. friend for his support and I will say so to the electors of Gaspe.
I suppose that the old G. N. Armstrong charter is abolished ?
The Armstrong charter covering all that ground as far as GaspS Basin has lapsed. This is a new company and lias nothing whatever to do with Mr. Armstrong. In fact it was fought by Mr. Armstrong.
Will this road touch all the improvements we have been making in Bonaventure and Gaspe ?
It will improve the improvements.

Are there any better prospects of this company building that road than there was of the Armstrong company building it ? The hon. gentleman has vigorously fought the old company for years and I would like to know if he is substituting anything better.

I think so ; I can assure my hon. friend that the government and the two members most interested, the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and myself, have taken all the precautions that were possible. In fact, I am positive that within the year we will have at least ten or twenty miles built. The gentlemen are quite in earnest and have the financial ability to carry out the project.
Who are the gentlemen ?
What is the object of this ? I understand that it is running out to a mill owned by an hon. member of this House.
If an hon. member of this House is fortunate enough to own a mill I think we ought to be glad of it. We do not expect the members of this House to be dummies, but energetic business men.
The rule with us is that when you want a siding you build it yourself.

This is a spur at a point near River Trois Pistoles on the Intercolonial Railway to Mackenzie and Renouf Falls, RiviSre Trois Pistoles. A large pulp mill is being built there and there "are also large timber limits.
In what county is that ? The MINISTER OF FINANCE. In Temi-scouata.
Who is the owner of this large pulp mill that is to be built there ?
It is a joint stock company of which Mr. Tobin, member I for Richmond and Wolfe is president.

I regard this as a very improper way to use public money. A year or two ago a subsidy was proposed for the Manitoulin and North Shore Railway, which goes through my county, and a portion of that goes through the township of St. Vincent and town of Meaford. It was proposed to build the Grand Trunk Railway down into the town of Meaford which would be probably two and a half miles and although a subsidy was given from that town to build around to Owen Sound and one end of this road would start practically at the wharf and the other extend towards Owen Sound, and although I did my best to get the government to allow a portion of that subsidy to apply to the building of the road down to the wharf, about one and a half or two miles from the end of the Grand Trunk Railway I was answered that the government was not subsidizing or using public money in that way, that this was only a short spur down to the wharf and that the people of the town should build it or that it should be built between them and the railway company. The people were obliged, notwithstanding the fact that a subsidy was given professedly to build a railway from that point, to raise the money to build it themselves. The government would not allow a dollar of the subsidy to be applied in that way and now we are asked to vote a subsidy to assist in building a spur or siding into a man's mill. Because that man happens to be a member of this House he is treated in this way. If these subsidies were given alike in all cases I would not have the same ground for complaint, but where it is emphatically denied in other cases upon grounds which if applied to this case would exclude this gentleman from such benefits, then I think it is unfair and that we have a right to object to it.

I do not remember the other case to which my hon. friend refers, but, it is a mistake to refer to this as a siding; this is not a siding; it is a line that runs off almost at right angles with the Intercolonial Railway at a place where it is believed there will be a considerable development of business. Whether it is a proper subsidy to grant is a debatable matter, but it is not right to describe this line as a siding.

In our country if a man wants a siding or spur into his mill he has to go to the cost of constructing it and the company charges him interest on the rails, besides which he has to maintain the spur. Here the government is to build a road which is really a part of the Intercolonial Railway and is paying a subsidy.
It is practically a man building a railway into his mill and getting $7,000 to do it. If you would apply the same principle all over the country I would not have the same objection to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: In what year was the application of which my hon. friend has spoken, made ?

There is a principle involved in this case. Why should we, the ratepayers as a whole, be called upon to build two and a half miles of a spur or siding, whatever you call it, for the benefit of a member of this House ? Why should we vote public money for the benefit of a private individual or company. If a railway is developing a country, I would not oppose a subsidy for it no matter in what province it may be, but the government has practically gone insane in voting subsidies this year for little dabs of railways one mile and two miles long, to serve private individuals. The Prime Minister himself must see that this is absurd. Why don't these people do as we have to do in our section of the country, where these railways are built by the private individuals who want them. When these gentlemen on the other side of the House were in opposition, they objected to the name of a member of parliament appearing as an applicant for a charter, but now they sit complacently by and vote this money when a member of the government makes an application to the Minister of Finance for a subsidy. It looks to me a little fishy, and it is time we called a halt. We have gone so far to-day as to subsidize local roads that are chartered by the provincial government, and now we are subsidizing roads which serve the purposes only of some private corporation. How cau the members for Ontario go home and justify themselves in voting subsidies for these little tramp railways down in the provinces, when in our own province private individuals have to build their own roads ? If this were a colonization road I could understand it ; but there is no reason on earth why a man should not build his own siding to his mill.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: As I understand it, this is a branch of the Intercolonial Railway which runs into some industrial establishments lying along that line. Is it the intention of the government to loan them the rails in addition to giving them this subsidy ?
There is no arrangement whatever between the Intercolonial Railway and this company. This is treated as an ordinary subsidy.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: To whom ?
To the company.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Will this road bei operated by that independent company or by the Intercolonial Railway ?
There has been no arrangement yet on the subject.

The acting Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Fielding) objected to this road being called a siding, but 1 find that in the application which was made by the company themselves, they designated it both as a siding and a spur line. Here is what they say :
Application to construct a spur line near the Trois Pistoles bridge.
Oh, oh.

And here is the letter written to the engineer of the Intercolonial Railway by the government engineer who was sent to inspect it.
As per instructions received from you, I went to Trois Pistoles to go over ground and make report on whait is to be a siding or branch from the Intercolonial Railway to a point up stream, where a company own timber limits and water privileges on the main River Trois Pistoles. I found a preliminary location survey has been made by an engineer, sent there by Mr. Tobin and his company. I walked over ground in company with their engineer. The proposed branch or siding is about two and a half miles in length and begins at a point on the Intercolonial Railway about 700 feet east of Trois Pistoles bridge ; running south, crossing the public highway at about grade point, keeping the side hill, passing two large grist mills.
There is one feature of this subsidy which I dislike very much. The general public are not allowed to participate in the advantages of this railway at all ; they will get no benefit from the construction of this railway ; the private company will receive all the benefit. I object to these subsidies for a line simply to run into a granite quarry, to satisfy the desires of a minister ol' the Crown or any other persons with, whom he may be associated. This company tells the government that they have acquired all the water privileges and all the land within a very considerable distance, so that everybody else except the company is excluded from participating in the benefits of (his expenditure. This letter is a lengthy one, and I shall not detain the House by reading more than a portion of it. It says :
The company of which Mr. Tobin is promoter proposes building at once at terminus of branch, a large pulp mill, a shingle mill, and an electric power house. And at McKenzie's Palls, about
1.000	feet below, erecting a large paper mill. The electric .power house is for the purpose of lighting all the mills on stream below, two large grist mills, and Messrs. Price Bros, large saw mill, and also to light the town of Trois Pistoles by electricity. The company here have acquired all water privileges up this river for a distance of ten mies and have also control of
100.000	acres of timber limits situated on both sides of Trois Pistoles river and extending back in country considerable distance a,nd have control of all available timber lands for some miles back.
They have everything in sight.

That is the great objection. This company has oblained pos-453
session of everything in sight; no other person can go in there and acquire water privileges or piece of land, without dealing with this company. All the benefits which accrue from this subsidy must of necessity go to the company. It is a close corporation, and all the benefits the public get from it. is what may be doled out to the workingman in the shape of wages. It is altogether a -wrong1 principle to subsidize such a road as this. No doubt these 100,000 acres of land, and this long stretch of water-power privilege was obtained before there was a railway there, and at a cheap price because of the difficulty of access ; but when this company became possessed of everything in sight, they go to the government and ask them to spend $10,000 or $15,000 to make this property more valuable. They bought it at a cheap price because there was no railway connection, and now they want the government to give them railway connection, so as to enhance its value. Had the subsidy been granted before this company'acquired all the property there would be some fair play in it, because then others would have an opportunity of going in there and acquiring property on the same basis. This in undoubtedly a case which has no merit in it whatever. If these people want a siding two and a half miles long, let them do as we have to do in the province of Ontario. I know very well that in the province of Ontario when we want a siding on the Canadian Pacific Railway, we have to make the embankment, put- on the ties, and pay a considerable rental for the iron.
Any rebate allowed ?

No rebate at all. We pay the regular freight ail the same. I am not finding fault with this. I cannot expect the Canadian Pacific Railway to provide special privileges without being compensated for them. But we do not come to the government and ask them to give us these facilities. In the constituency I have the honour to represent, I know of a spur line which was built from the main line of the Grand Trunk Railway to a paper mill. The hon. member for Nipissing has been pleading here all afternoon in favour of supporting grants to paper and pulp mills. There is a very large and old paper mill in the constituency I have the honour to represent, and I do not think it ever secured aid for the construction of railway facilities for bringing out its output. A few years ago a spur line was built from the Grand Trunk to the mill. I cannot say whether it was done at the expense of the proprietors or at the expense of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. 1 am inclined to think that the proprietor had to assist ; but I am quite sure that the government were not asked to contribute one cent, although that was as meritorious a case as the one we have before us now. The



proprietor of that mill and his predecessors for the last forty or fifty years hare employed a great deal of labour ; their output is very considerable ; and if a paper or pulp mill is entitled to consideration, that one is as much entitled to it as those in newer sections of the country. I disapprove altogether of aiding private enterprises of this kind where the general public are excluded from taking any advantage of the investment. I do not think this case has any merit at all.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

With regard to the item 53, now before the committee, for a branch line to Mackenzie and Renouf Falls, river Trois Pistoles, not exceeding 2| miles, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) asked what arrangement was made with the Intercolonial regarding the rails to be laid on that siding. It is surely not proposed to hand over to a private company-not a railway company at all-all these compensations. As pointed out by my hon. friend, they have grabbed everything in sight. They have secured the water-power and the timber limits and every concession possible before investing a dollar in the way of plant, and they ask the country now to construct a railway for them.
There is no arrangement whatever between the government and this company with respect to the operation of the road. The subsidy is the same as any other subsidy and in no different position.
It is in a very different position from all others.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the company have not spent anything at Trois Pistoles ?
There is no plant there.
In my constituency, Temiscouata, $250,000 have been spent. There are three shingle mills in operation.
How long have the mills been in operation ?
Two months. We expect to have five shingle mills at work, and in one year will export 1,200 cars of lumber by the Intercolonial.
Is this Mr. Tobin's company ?
It is an American company. The promoters are French Canadians from the States, and Mr. Tobin is the president. Those who have invested the most money are French Americans.

We are very glad to welcome them back to this country, and to
welcome the investment of capital in Canada, but there is no reason why the Canadian tax-payer should build sidings for Mr. Tobin or anybody else. We might as well build the mills for his company. This siding is essentially a part of the plant of the company, in which the public are not interested. This company want the government to build a road for them and at the same time loan them the rails and give them the balance of the outfit. We ought to know on what arrangement they are to get these other advantages apart from the subsidy.	.

The hon. gentleman is making much ado about something which he considers entirely novel. I can assure him that he is mistaken. The grant of a subsidy for a small road-call it a siding if you will, but it is not a siding- two or three miles long, is by no means a novelty either under the present or former administrations. This company cannot do everything, and there will be a large population gathered around their industries which will give business to the railway. As to how the Intercolonial will arrange with the company later on, that is a matter for future adjustment.

There is a wide distinction between this and other grants to railways. This is not a road which the public can use. It is a private road in every sense of the word. If we are to take this subsidy as a precedent, there is not a mill-owner in Canada who is not entitled to have a siding built to his mill by the government.
Why do you not move to strike it out ?

That is just the kind of suggestion I would expect from the hon. gentleman. He always throws a stone from behind the hedge and never comes out in the open. Did he ever move to strike out an item of that kind when contending against it ? If he did not, why does he ask me to move ?
I never whined for a' couple of hours over an item.

The hon. gentleman has whined over matters of much less importance, and the hilarity which his interruption excites, particularly on the part of the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Calvert), who had lame men in his riding employed as census enumerators, who had to be carried around in the villages to do the work, is very amusing. The fact that this is a small matter does not at all improve the quality of it. Members cannot come to this House and make demands for votes of public money for the benefit of concerns in which they are personally interested without violating a well recognized .principle of our parliamentary system.

This is the feature of it that it seems to me without a single redeeming side. I do not- expect to get better information than we have had, but I suppose that hon. gentlemen opposite will have to deal with the public later on.

We have been voting railway subsidies pretty freely, and very seldom have we on this side offered any serious objection to what was proposed, if there was anything like a justification for the vote. But in the multiplicity of these proposals, it cannot be wondered at that some do not meet with our approval. If we are to support the expenditure of public money it must be upon the basis of some reasonable belief that the expenditure will benefit the public, not an individual or a corporation alone, but the people. It never was proposed, so far as I know, that a subsidy should be given to a private firm or company to build a siding into their mill. Some years ago I applied to the government for some assistance by way of subsidy to build a line from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway to an important village in our county. The distance would be about two or two and a half miles. We had the assurance of parties who were well able to carry out the work that if the government would give the usual subsidy of $3,200 a mile they would build the line to the village. It was an important village, a place that had been settled for forty years or so ; it contained a grist mill, a saw mill, a woollen mill and the usual other industries of a thriving village, as well as stores of all kinds. With all these, its trade was a very considerable trade indeed. I applied to the government for the subsidy and submitted the best arguments I could. But I was quietly told that such a subsidy would not be justified by the House, and that the minister would not feel justified in recommending it to the Council, for the reason that this was only a spur line. I was told that if I could show that the line would connect two railway systems, so that cars could be transferred from one to the other, it might he regarded as worthy of a subsidy. But, though the village might, be an important one and its trade large and growing, the conditions were not such as to justify the subsidy being granted. In view of that, I do not know how I am to go back to the same people and justify such a proposition as is made here, for this has far less merit in it in many respects. In this instance, practically everything in sight, the water-powers, the timber lands, the mill sites and everything else, is owned by a company, and the public have no substantial interest. We are not even told that this is a thickly settled country or that there are industries there in which the public are interested. But it would seem that this company has secured everything it can from the local government and. being still unsatisfied. it comes to the Dominion for fur-453*
ther assistance. For the purpose of carrying on their business they desire sidings to be 'built into their property, and they come to the government and ask for assistance to the extent of $7,000 or $8,000 for this purpose. It can well be admitted that this will be more profitable to the company, but I do not understand that it is even claimed that it is of any substantial benefit to the public. It seems to me that the government have wholly failed to make out a case in favour of this vote. They have not even told us that this railway is owned by a regularly chartered railway company, or whether this *road is to be built by the Intercolonial under the general provision of the Railway Act, which gives a company the right to build branches not more than six miles in length without special charter. The hon. member-(Mr. Gauvreau), who seems to be familiar with the locality, speaks of a eompany- Mr. Tobin's company. I did not understand whether it was a railway company, a general commercial company or a lumber company.
It is a lumber company.

So, no railway company wants this, but merely an association of capitalists engaged in the lumber business. Let me tell the acting Minister of Railways (Hon.
