Mr. Fielding) that if he adopts this principle to-night and we vote this railway subsidy, he can have at once a thousand applications equally meritorious from all parts of the country. And if he grants this, how can he refuse the others ? It seems to me that this is establishing a very bad precedent a precedent that the government of this country will find very troublesome in the future.

The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says that we are establishing a bad precedent in this case. Now, I do not know the merits of this case very well, but I contend that the precedent for it was established long years ago.
When ?
By the late government. And the hon. member for East Grey has, over and over again, supported propositions just the same as this.
Give an instance.
The Cape Tormentine Railway.	1
I emphatically deny that I ever supported a proposition of this kind, knowing it to be such.
Oh, oh.

Let me say one word in explanation. Many of these railway subsidies were voted, the exact locality and merits of which we could not know. I may have supported such a proposition under these circumstances, but not under any other.
But the hem. gentleman supported it just the same ; and if he did not know what he was supporting, he was not tit to occupy
Tell me an instance.
If the hon. gentleman will look over the subsidies granted by the late government, he will iina many cases of grants in cases such as this.
Mention one.

I may say to the hon. gentleman for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) that I have already mentioned one. It was for Mr. Wood, who now occupies a position in the other House. He was supporting the government, and it was at his instance that [DOT] the subsidy was granted. It seems strange, therefore, that these men, when similar precedents have been established, and when they have over and over again voted bonuses to similar enterprises, should now rise in their righteous indignation and oppose this justifiable grant. The member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brook) will support bonuses where he is interested for $100,000 or $200,000. yet he will stick, and haggle and whine about a little tu'penny-ha'penny thing of two miles and a half that is in the public interest.

The hon. gentleman is putting his foot in it now. I am not whining about this at all, and I defy him to mention a ease where I supported a bonus that I am interested in myself. He is making a statement that he must know to be uot according to the facts.

When hon. members sit in this House and allow subsidies to go through without a protest, without raising their voice against them, we may rightly conclude that they are in favour of them. Therefore, when they advocate certain bonuses, and do not vote against others, they are responsible for their passage. The proper way for a member of this House to do, if he is opposed to a grant and has the courage of his convictions, is to rise in the House and move that the item he struck out. That would be the duty of those hon. gentlemen who oppose this grant as the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) does so strongly ; he should rise in his place and move that the item be struck out, then he will be acting according to his convictions.

We are asked to name a case. I will give the case of what is known as the Harvey branch, which connects the Albert Railway, now known as the Salisbury and Harvey, with a private wharf which was owned by the late Hon. J. .T. S. Turner. He owned this branch, and he owned the wharf, and the parliament of Canada, somewhere in the 80's, under a Conservative administration, not only subsidized that siding down to the wharf, but gave assistance to a bridge.
What was the length of the branch ?
Between two and three miles, about the same length as the branch in question. But he was a Tory, he was a member of a Tory government.

The hon. member has not made good his statement that it was a similar case, because in that instance the grant was given to a railway company, whereas this is being given to a commercial company.
The MINISTER OB' FINANCE. This is not being given to any company.
The hon. gentleman explained it as being given to the Tobin Company, which he admits is not a railway company. Who applied for it ? Is it not the Tobin Company ?
The Harvey branch was owned by one man. the gentleman I referred to, and it was no more of a publicrailway than this is to be.
There are many railways owned by only one man, and we have already voted subsidies to connect railways with a wharf
Not a private wharf.

We have wharfs by the dozen that are private wharfs, but the public use them all the time to ship their produce. Though this railway may have been owned by one man, it was for the public convenience to connect a water route and land route. Therefore it is not a similar case.
That branch was built for the purpose of permitting the gentleman who owned this wharf to ship his lumber down to that wharf over this branch or siding.
Did not the public use it as well as himself, both for incoming and outgoing freight ?
I presume the public-will use this in the same way.

Well it is not very likely. Now, the member for West York (Mr. Campbell), with his usual inaccuracy and braggadocio, says, I am going to give a ease, and he cites the case of Senator Wood. Well, did Senator Wood get a subsidy either as a private individual or as a corporation ? I deny it, and the hon. gentleman cannot confirm his statement. It was given to a railway company for the convenience of the public, and not to a private individual or a private corporation.

I want to say that the Cape Tormentine Railway has nothing to do with the item which we are discussing. That railway received a charter be-casue it goes for 18 or 20 miles through a

very populous district, and serves a great number of people, while the instance under discussion is a private corporation which controls the whole river, which controls the whole area of timber limits, and the whole situation. It is simply a private individual. The Cape Tormentine Railway was also built to connect the winter service of Prince Edward Island with Cape Tormentine.
The ease I refer to is several years old. The railway, as I remember, was a siding that went into Mr. \\ ood's sawmill, and was about a mile and a half long.

I do not know anything about Mr. Wood's sawmill. The hon. gentleman referred to the Cape Tormentine Railway, and I think there is no fair comparison with this item. While I am on this subject, and as I see the leader of the government in his seat, I would like to refer to the need of branch lines in Prince Edward Island. While we are giving subsidies to hundreds of branch lines throughout this Dominion, we have been unsuccessfully asking in Prince Edward Island for branch lines through populous districts, to serve the farming community, to serve cheese factories, and butter factories, and manufacturing industries throughout the Island. I have instanced a number of cases, and I have presented petition after petition in this House, with no result. During the three years I have been here I have presented petitions for a branch line from North Wiltshire to the southern coast, through a populous district, a line about twenty miles long, a line that will serve a great number of persons. I have also brought to the attention of the acting Minister of Railways and Canals another branch that was needed down to Elmira, and a branch from O'Leary to the western part of the Island. These branches are all much needed by a great number of people. I would like the leader of the government to take these matters in hand. The main line is a government line, and if we are going to get any railway accommodation at all we must get it through branch lines built by the government. While on the subject of short branch lines, I would also mention that I have brought to the attention of the acting Minister of Railways this year, as the board of trade of the maritime provinces have also done, the need of a spur running from the main line at Charlottetown down to the wharf front, which would serve not one private individual, but the whole commercial community of Charlottetown. And during the season of navigation, when the goods are brought into Charlottetown to private wharfs, every bit of that merchandise has to be carted across the town to the station at Charlottetown at a greatly increased cost and at great inconvenience to the shippers. We have been asking for a spur that would not be two and a half miles long and possibly would not be over one mile in length, and yet we have
been put off from year to year with the explanation that ' we will look into the case.' I wish that the acting minister would look into it with some seriousness.
There is no relevancy at all in the observations of my hon. friend.
There is a great deal of relevancy in them.

We are dealing with railway subsidies, we are not dealing with the construction of railways by the government. There has been no application from anybody in Prince Edward Island to my knowledge for the privileges which are proposed to be conferred on railway companies or other parties by these votes, and any discussion of the construction of branches by the Intercolonial Railway has no relevancy to this. These gentlemen would be very pleased indeed if we would build then a branch line of railway ; but the government do not propose to build them a branch line, simply to offer them tlie usual facilities in the way of subsidies and for the rest they must pay the money themselves. If any one in Prince Edward island wants the same privileges on the same conditions I fancy that the government would be ready to grant it, but, there is no such proposal from Prince Edward island and there is no relevancy in the point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey). If the hon. gentleman wants to advocate the building of a branch line in Prince Edward Island it would he a very proper subject at tlie proper time. If lie wants to convey the impression that this government lias not been dealing liberally with the province of Prince Edword Island, I am satisfied that there Is too much common sense among the people of that island, in view of tlie appropriations contained in the estimates for that province, to permit the people to treat ills remarks seriously.

We are dealing with the public money of this country, and it makes no difference whether it is being expended for subsidies or for tlie building of lines. We do not ask for subsidies in Prince Edward Island ; we do not build branch lines in Prince Edward Island because the whole system is owned by the government.
So is the Intercolonial Railway in this case.

We want the government to build a line there, as they own the whole system and for that reason the subject is perfectly relevant; it is the expenditure of public money to suit the convenience of the people in the locality and to assist them in carrying on the enterprise in which they are engaged. This spur line in Charlottetown would not only lie a convenience to the shippers of produce, &c.. in Charlottetown, hut would benefit the Prince Edward Island Railway.

The MINISTER OF1 FINANCE. The hon. gentleman is trying to convey the impression that by these subsidy resolutions some privilege is being granted to other provinces that is not granted to Prince Edward Island.
They certainly are.
They certainly are not, because no one in Prince Edward Island has sought the privileges that are granted by this.
They cannot.

It is no more impracticable for them than for people living along the line of the Intercolonial Railway. If' the hon. gentleman says that subsidies are refused to his province, he is wrong ; but if he is not seising railway subsidies how can he complain if he does not get them.

The hon. Minister of Finance seems to be worked up on the question of irrelevancy. He did not seem to be so much concerned about irrelevancy when the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) got up and referred to something done many years ago by another government.
By a subsidy I understood.

We might infer from the words of the hon. member for West York that if a minister twenty years ago had picked a man's pocket that would justify the right hon. gentleman who now leads the government in committing a burglary. That seems to be his argument. The Minister of Finance says this is not a matter affecting the Intercolonial Railway ; it is a matter of public concern, a subsidy to be granted by this Dominion. I think the facts are just the reverse of what the Minister of Finance states. This is particularly a matter affecting the Intercolonial Railway, and I think it is absolutely ridiculous for an hon. gentleman to stand up in this House and say that a two and a half mile side track on the Intercolonial Railway is a matter affecting the Dominion, for which a Dominion subsidy ought to be granted. If this is a siding or a spur track that is useful to the Intercolonial Railway why has not the Minister of Railways and Canals dealt with it ? If that hon. gentleman, as acting Minister of Railways and Canals, thinks that this two and a half mile track is a necessity for the Intercolonial Railway, surely he could have dealt with that subject as a railway manager deals with every application of the kind. The very fact that it has not been -brought up in that way, that the Minister of Railways and Canals has not so dealt with this two and a half spur track Mr. LEFURGEY.
to a timber limit, owned by a private Individual, is the strongest possible evidence that we can have that this is not a matter that ought to be paid for by the Dominion at large. The hon. gentleman could, if he nad chosen, have dealt with this as he has dealt with many other cases where the Intercolonial Railway is interested in a side-track for a spur track or anything of that kind. If he thought the business with this private commercial enterprise justified the Intercolonial Railway in connecting its line with that enterprise by a side track; he could have dealt with it by (agreement. The people interested in that enterprise would have entered into a contract with the government and would have undertaken to pay to the government the cost of that siding. Probably there has been some side influence in this case which leads the government not to deal with it, as the Grand Trunk Railway or Canadian Pacific Railway or any other large railway company would deal with such a case; the hon. gentleman has not dealt with it as a departmental matter but has turned it over to the Dominion, and he gravely asks parliament to grant a subsidy for two and a half miles of railway as if a connection with this private timber limit were in the interests of the whole of the Dominion.

It seems to me that the immortal feature of this transaction should command the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals. The law governing the independence of parliament provides that no member of parliament can receive money from the country and the only way in which he can evade the consequences of the law is by being connected with a company. The principle we have laid down is that we will assist railways, but in this case we are departing from the salutary principle and now we are going to help commercial companies to build railways into their own premises. I want to submit this feature :	How can Mr. Tobin, who is a
member of this House, be an independent member of parliament and vote against any government measure during this session when he is a suppliant at the door of the government for this subsidy ? How can lie be expected to do so ? It is not in human nature to expect it. It is unreasonable, and while Mr. Tobin may not deliberately violate the independence of parliament Act he is actually violating the spirit of it if not the letter. No member of parliament can be as independent as he should be when he is here seeking a subsidy of money from which he himself will be the principle beneficiary and the largest share of which will go into his own pocket. It seems to me that the government should refrain from doing that kind of thing and that this is a very bad precedent and an improper thing to do.

My bon. friend (Mr. Sproule) worries his soul over

the morals of the members In this respect. How does he justify one of his colleagues who sits usually immediately behind him and who is a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, although we are voting subsidies to the Canadian Pacific Railway ? My hon. friend does not worry over that member's morals in the slightest degree.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has ever known the hon. gentleman to whom he refers to sit in this House and vote upon the question of a bonus to the railway to which he refers ?

I did not discuss that question. Mr. Tobin, the hon. member for Richmond and Wolfe is not sitting in this House, voting on this question, yet his name has been used freely, more freely than I have used the name of the hon. the junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier). It seems to make a great difference whose ox is gored. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is very much worried because some of these votes are not expressly to	railway companies. It would be a dreadful thing if we should vote money to any company that is not a railway company. This is not a vote to any company, it is a vote for a line of railway. It is in the same position as any other line of railway where no company is mentioned. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) was not always so squeamish about these things as he is now. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) says that if some one picked some one else's pocket years ago, that would not justify another person in committing a burglary now. No, but if a person who committed a burglary years ago, suddenly becomes virtuous, and howls when another person commits a burglary, there is something very suspicious about it.
We are not looking for virtue from that side.
The hon. gentleman expects all the virtue to be on this side of the House.
We are complaining that there is no virtue on that side of the House.

We are just ordinary plain people over here, and we do not profess to have that high degree of morality, which enables us to single out the member for Richmond and Wolfe, to lecture him on morals, without looking at the vacant seat behind the hon. member for East Grey. But if there is any degree in morals, we suspect Strongly that the member for Richmond and Wolfe is not the bigger sinner in these transactions. I find that in 1888, a vote was made of rails and fastenings ; which are money ; which stood in the public accounts as an asset for $4,335; these were voted, not to assist a railway company, but to assist a cotton company in the city of Halifax. That is commonly known in my city as the cotton factory
siding, and this line was built for the special advantage of the Halifax Cotton Company. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) told us the other night that he was here for a quarter of a century, and we were all glad to congratulate him
Might I ask the hon. minister if that was not an arrangement made with the Intercolonial Railway ?
The Intercolonial Railway is the government -of Canada.
It is a different thing altogether.

It does not make it any better or any worse, whether it was an arrangement made with the Intercolonial Railway or not, and I have a pretty strong suspicion-but I do not like to mention names without having an opportunity to verify the record-I have a pretty strong suspicion that some of the members of parliament who sat here when that subsidy was voted, were members of the Halifax Cotton Company. But right alongside that last vote, I find that another appropriation is made of rails and fastenings, which are money, which stood in the public acounts as an asset representing $11,964.56. Was that voted in blank to someone else with the possibility of getting it taken up by an incorporated railway company ? No, it was voted to a company which was not a railway company, but which was known as the Steel Company of Canada. This grant was given for a branch, or a siding to their factory.
What were the general conditions in connection with that ?
The only general condition is, that they would put down a certain quantity of rails themselves.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And all for the benefit of the Intercolonial Railway.
This proposed vote will be for the benefit of the Intercolonial Railway ; this is a branch of the Intercolonial Railway. What is the difference ?
Will the hon. minister allow me to ask him a question ? Will the hon. gentleman say that the rails he refers to there are not to-day the property of the Intercolonial Railway ?

I cannot tell, but I can tell that these resolutions granted the rails to the Halifax Cotton Company, and to the Steel Company of Canada. Here is what it says :
To the Halifax Cotton Company of Nova Scotia, a grant as subsidy-the road to be first laid with new steel rails weighing not less than 56 pounds per lineal yard, and after an Order in Council has been passed authorizing their transfer to the company-of 233 tons of used iron rails and fastenings, loaned to the company



Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

Hold on: they first loaned them, and that was not bad enough as a matter of .morals, but they went further and then gave them afterwards.
-two hundred and thirty-three tons of used iron rails and fastenings loaned to the company, which rails and fastenings stand in the public accounts as an asset for $4,335.
This is a grant to the Halifax Cotton Company.

It is a loan.
The MINISTER OF FINA'NCE. No ; it says they have already been loaned, but this is a grant.
Could the Steel Company or the Cotton Company dispose of these rails as being their property ?

It is a grant given to them here. If there is a grant of anything given to the hon. gentleman by vote of this parliament, he can do as he likes with it. We have it plainly stated :
To the Halifax Cotton Company of Nova Scotia a grant as subsidy. &c.

The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well, that what he has read is the ordinary transaction whereby a railway company issues its old second-hand rails as a loan to an enterprise that it wants to assist, by allowing a siding. They lend their rails, but the rails belong to the company lending them, and the siding cannot he used for any other purpose than for connection with the railway that lends the rails. Hoes the hon. gentleman suppose, that in addition to that resolution which he has read, there is not a contract with the Intercolonial Railway, that the Intercolonial Railway does not control that siding as any railway company controls the sidings that are made to connect with its main line ? The hon. gentleman knows that is probably the case. But what is the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) doing by this resolution which we are considering ? He is giving a subsidy in hard cash to a private individual who is building two and a half miles of track, and that individual, whoever he may be, will receive that money in his own pocket.

The hon. gentleman does no credit to his professional ingenuity when he makes such a weak argument as that. This is a grant to the Halifax Cotton Company and the Canada Steel Company. It is not anything but a grant. We have to take it just as we find it: as my hon. friend has just to take what he finds in the present resolution. We are proposing to grant certain aid to this road down at Trois Pistoles. In these resolutions I have quoted, the government

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: of the day brought to parliament a proposal to grant aid, and whether they granted it in rails or cash it made no difference, because the rails represented cash, and it is stated here that they stood in the assets of Canada as so much cash, and they must be brought down to the basis of hard pan in cash value.

The hon. gentleman knows that the Railway Department of that day had no power whatever to lend these rails, without coming to parliament and getting authority. They came here and they got authority to lend these rails for the purpose of that siding. If the hon. gentleman will undertake to state that that was an absolute gift of these rails, I have nothing further to say. But the hon. minister has admitted that lie cannot say that. The langauge he has read from the resolution does not show more than that parliament had authorized the granting a loan of rails to that company.

My hon. friend is mistaken. The resolution distinctly states that these rails are granted to the company. These rails had already been loaned to tbe company, and it did not need an Act of parliament to loan tbern.
Certainly it did.
Then they had loaned them before, and whether they had loaned them by an Act of parliament or not I do not know.
They loaned them without authority, and they had to come to parliament to get the authority.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) is standing here to abuse tbe late government, by saying that it did these things without authority.
Certainly.

I protest against this attempt of the hon. gentleman to escape responsibility by attacking the late government. I do not believe the late government would do such thing. I do not believe they would lend the property of the Crown without authority. I am bound to believe that the minister of that day, who, I think, was the hon. member for Lanark (lion. Mr. Haggart) was a man who observed the law and in his absence to-night I want to defend him against this calumny.
He does'nt want your defence.

The resolution distinctly states that it is to be a grant of 233 tons of used iron rails and fastenings loaned to the company. They already had them. They were In their possession ; they were loaned to them ,and this resolution gives them a free gift, and it gives that gift to them at the net cash price in which it stood in the assets of Canada.

I wish to draw attention to the comparison that the acting minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) has made between this case and the case of the member for Toronto (Mr. Osier), who is a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Let me point out that the Canadian Pacific Railway is a railway which is over 4,000 miles long.
How does that affect the question of morals ?

It affects the question of morals a great deal. This is a railway of 4,000 miles, which has its ramifications all over Canada, supplying the needs of the people, and handling the commerce of the country whether it be the product of the farm or the product of the manufacturer. That company which is engaged in building a highway of commerce for the people of every part of Canada, deserves assistance from this government. There is an hon. member of this House who happens to be a member of that corporation, and because a subsidy is given to that great international railway enterprise, the Minister of Finance thinks that member is as guilty as the member who receives a subsidy for no railway corporation whatever, and a subsidy which is not given for the beneiit of tin1 public, but for the private beneiit of that member. It does not ask a dollar of it for the accommodation of the public. The public have no interest there, because this corporation owns the land, the timber, the water-power and everything else in the locality.
That is what the Canadian Pacific Railway does when it gets a chance.

It is begging the question to cite that as a parallel case. It is a very unfair comparison to say that the hon. member for West Toronto is doing an equally immoral act to sit in this Plouse when a subsidy is being voted the Canadian Pacific Railway, as the member who represents this company, and who goes to the government and asks for this bonus. It goes largely, you might almost say solely, into his own pocket, whereas the Canadian Pacific Railway is building railroads all over the country.
What year was it in which that loan of rails was made ?
I cannot say in what year the loan was made, but the year from which I quoted was 1888.

I desire to call the attention of the House to the rather peculiar circumstance that the acting Minister of Railways and Canals justifies this grant for two and a half miles of railway by a precedent of fifteen years ago. The hon. gentleman has been looking up the records. He has felt that this subsidy is something very unusual; he has been conscious that he had to
justify it, and he has looked back fifteen years to find a case which would justify what he is doing ; and what has he found? He has come here with a report of 1888, and lie has taken very good care not to look into the agreement entered into then to ascertain whether it was a loan or not.
The Act fixes that.

In reference to this loan of rails to the Steel Company of Canada, having some knowledge of the matter, I wish to state that these rails were taken by the steel company, put on their own land, treated as their own property, the company went into liquidation, its assets were sold, and among the assets sold were these same rails.
They were not loaned ; they were granted, and the company had a right to sell them.

The acting Minister of Railways gave my hon. friend from Prince a distinct challenge, and I understood him to say that if application were made from Prince Edward Island under similar conditions, it would be granted. I want to ask the hon. gentleman now if he has dealt with every case of a siding along the Intercolonial Railway in the same manner in which this is being dealt with. If the hon. gentleman is following out a rule that has obtained for many years, whether it is a good rule or a bad one, he will have some excuse for the course he is taking.

Let me first note the remark of the hon. .gentleman that I said that if an application were made from Prince Edward Island, the same privilege would be granted. I did not say that. I said it would be time enough to consider an application from Prince Edward Island when the application came. So far we have not had any.
The hon. gentleman is not so generous as I thought he was.

I do not want to be generous ; I want to be reasonable. I want to point out that I have no right to promise in the name of the government that these things will he done. When applications come forward each one will be dealt with on its merits, and one province will be treated as well as another. The hon. gentleman wants to know if we are dealing with all these cases alike. Yes. where subsidies have been granted for small branch roads, they are granted in the same way ; and my hon. friend sat in this House yesterday and voted-and I am glad he did- for the following item :
For a line of railway from Debert station on the Intercolonial Railway to Coal Mine, not excoding 4f miles.
A difference of a mile or two makes no difference, and if I had time to go through the books I could find a number of cases

in wliieli small branch lines have received subsidies. I think I have answered the hon. gentleman's question.
The hon. gentleman has not answered it at all.
Not in the way the hon. gentleman wanted.

The way I want is a direct answer to a direct question. The hon. gentleman has so far evaded it. I shall repeat the question again. There are constant applications for sidings or branch lines ; you may call them either. Has it been the policy in the past and is it still the policy of the government of the day to treat all these applications alike ? If the hon. gentleman is prepared to admit that that is not the case, he is out of court.

I have not been dealing with the question of sidings. I am confining myself to branches, and I am pointing out that in granting a subsidy to aid a road two and a half miles in length, we are not doing anything that is new.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman, if after the railway is finished, this company which owns this timber and this land, exercises the privilege of selling the railroad as well as the land, will it become their property ?

This appropriation does not go to any particular company. It stands exactly in the same position as any other railway subsidy, and arrangem'ents would have to be made to have a contract as far as possible under the same terms and conditions as in the case of other subsidies. We have not made any arrangement which enables me to answer my hon. friend's question, except to state the general policy in relation to all roads of a like character.
Will this branch belong to the country or to this company, and will the subsidy raise the value of their property provided they want to sell it ?
It will stand in exactly the same position as all these other appropriations to companies. These roads will belong to the respective companies subject to the terms and conditions of the Railway Act.

I am asking the minister a very plain question, and I would like a plain answer. If this timber company sell the property shortly after the road is completed, will they sell the bonus which this country is giving them ?

It will stand in exactly the same position as any other railway company. It will be in the same condition as respects this bonus as the Canadian Pacific Railway will be with re-Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
spect to the $3,300,000 which we gave it for the Crow's Nest Railway. The principle is the same, the amount is nothing.

I am afraid that the next thing will be an application for money to buy out this branch of the Intercolonial. We will pay the subsidy and then buy the road back.
To the Matane and GaapS Railway Company for a line of railway from a point at or near St. Octave on the Intercolonial Railway to Matane. not exceeding 30 miles.
This is for a railway from the Intercolonial at Metis down to the St. Lawrence at Matane. The distance is thirty miles. There is no communication at all for these people after navigation Is closed.
Was there a company chartered for this ?
Yes. it has had a charter for several years.

I would like to find out how many lines of railway are subsidized by these resolutions in each of the provinces, and what is the aggregate of the money voted for each of the provinces respectively in these railway subsidies V

I have not made any statement from a provincial point of view.
Mr-. SPROULE. Could not the hon. gentleman get that ?
Is it necessary ? Why should we be provincial ?

It is not for the hou. gentleman to say whether it is necessary or not, if 1 desire the information. I am asking what is reasonable. There may be nothing wrong, and I am not saying there is ; but if it were only to satisfy ordinary curiosity, the question is a reasonable one to ask.
I am afraid that if I make out a statement by provinces, my own province will not look well, and I will be accused of having been unfair to it.

I want to get the information in some way or other and in other lines as well. We are entitled to it, so as to be able to make comparisons. It will not take much work for the hon. minister io get it if he desires to be agreeable.
I like to be agreeable.
Then the hon. gentleman will agree to give it ?
I had rather my hon. friend would make it himself. I might make at mistake and I want him to be responsible.

Tliat is a little lower than we would expect from the hon. gentleman, to treat a member of the House in that way. I do not think it is proper treatment. The question is a reasonable one and he can get the information in a short time.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to consider it and not ask me to make a promise ?
I want to know if I can get it. If I do not get it I will have to analyse these subsidies.
Do not stop, go on, we have not heard from the hon. gentleman this session.
Has the hon. gentleman awakened ?

We are in the eighth month of the session. The hon. gentleman has spoken several times every day these eight months. Do not deprive us of the pleasure of hearing him again in the dying moments. Let him continue to make himself a standing nuisance until the end of the session.

That statement is absolutely untrue. I tell the Postmaster General that to his face. He should be the last man to make such a statement. I am asking for what I regard as proper information and I desire to know whether I shall get it.

I do not think it is a very proper question, but ) am not refusing the request. I cannot prevent his getting the information because he can make out the statement himself. Therefore my answer does not prevent his getting It.

That is not treating hon. members with even ordinary courtesy. If the hon. gentleman had been asked something very unreasonable, I might be met with such a reply ; but I am not, and I respectfully submit that the ' put-off ' style of the hon. minister is not what we might expect from him. He has granted many more requests much more difficult to comply with. I want to know whether he is prepared to give this information, which he might easily get ?

We can both easily get it. My hon. friend and 1 and anybody else can get it in half an hour, but what I do not like is the hon. gentleman insisting on looking at these things from a provincial point of view. I know that he can take larger views. I do not refuse to give him the information, and he can get it even if I did refuse.

Only a few years ago we had a very lengthy discussion in which the right hon. the First Minister took part. The right hon. gentleman then showed conclusively to my judgment, that in the distribution of money for public works he had
made what I regarded as a very fair distribution among the provinces-much fairer than the Conservative party did when they were in power. In my own campaign I admitted that I believed it was a fair distribution. It was quite proper for the hon. gentleman to do that, and 1 do not see why it should be improper for me to go into the same inquiry. I am not contending that there is anything wrong, but 1 desire to ascertain how far the distribution of these subsidies complies with the principle laid down by the right hon. gentleman some years ago, which I thought perfectly defensible in every particular. Surely if I can point to so high an authority for dealing with the question in the manner I suggest, I am not making an unreasonable request.

In view of the very handsome manner in which my hon. friend has acknowledged that this government has made a very fair and equitable distribution of the public funds as regards the different provinces, I will give him the information he requires.
To the Chateauguay and Northern Railway Company for a line of railway from a point on its main line at or near L'Epiphanie. passing by way of the parish of St, Jacques d'Achigan to the village of Rawdon, not exceeding 16 miles.

At this moment there is a railway being built from Montreal to Joliette to join Montreal to the Great Northern at Joliette by way of the Bout de l'lle bridge, which is intended to provide for a branch from 1'Epiphanie up to the village of Rawdon in the county of Montcalm, which section of country is not provided at all with railways.
Is there a company prepared to build this ?
The company is described in the resolution-the Chateauguay and Northern.

Is any of the road built now ?
The PRIME MINISTER, The road is now under construction. This is a new branch.
For a line of railway from the line of the Montreal and Atlantic Railway Company at St. Guillau-me to the River Yamaska to join with the South Shore Railway, a distance not exceeding 12 miles.

This is a railways to connect two railways. There is a railway passing St. Guillaume, the name of which I have forgotten at the moment and another road, the South Shore Railway, and a bridge on the Yamaska to connect the two and serve this section of country. The distance is 12 miles.
The company has a portion of the road built ?

No. this is an I independent road. The South Shore skirts

the St. Lawrence, ibut St. Guillaume is inland.
For a line of railway from La Tuque on the St. Maurice river to a point on the Lake St. John Railway near the River Jeannotte, not exceeding 35 imiles.

The Lake St. John Railway, as I explained on a previous vote, runs from Quebec to Lake St. John. This proposed railway is a branch westward, from a point on the Lake St. John road to the St. Maurice river, opening up a new section of country. It will be a good colonization road.
Is there a charter for the road ?
I am informed that there is. *
A provincial charter ?

I understand so. but I have no personal knowledge.
To the Montreal Northern Railway Company for a line of railway from a point at or near Ste. Agathe des Monts station towards the township of Howard, in the county of Argenteuil, passing near Lake St. Joseph.
This is a colonization road entirely.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Starting from Montreal ?

No, but from Ste. Agathe des Monts, 63 miles from Montreal. It opens up a country that has neither railway nor water communication. Half the road is already built, having begun early in the spring. The charter is a local one.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Has the
local government given assistance to this road ?
Not a cent as yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
If the local government gives the charter, and a subsidy is needed, the local government should begin the subsidizing. If a further subsidy is needed this government may be appealed to. But it is not a .good condition of things to have the charter granted iby the local government and then the company come here for assistance. If this is a local line, it should not get a Dominion subsidy. It certainly should not receive a subsidy unless the province gives one.
To the Beersville Coal and Railway Company for a line of railway from Adamsville on the Intercolonial Railway to a point at or near Brown's Landing or Beersville, not exceeding seven miles.

This line is intended to open up a new coal district. There have been some operations in coal mining in New Brunswick in recent years, and it is represented that there is a deposit Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
of coal near Adamsville, in tire county of Kent. This is to assist the line to develop the mining.
This is one subsidy that is justified by the circumstances.
Hear. bear.

I am glad to see that that brings a smile to the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite. The fact is that this railway will enable the Intercolonial to obtain coal much more cheaply than at present. They must now haul coal from Nova Scotia, but, with this road built, they will be able to get coal of a superior quality and much more conveniently. Of course, it would be much better if the Intercolonial would build this road themselves. That would be my choice by all means. I believe that the Intercolonial should own all these branches. They should own the Central Railway, the Albert Railway, the Kent Northern and all these different branches. These roads could be operated much more cheaply than at present, for one staff would do for all, and" they could be operated much more beneficially to the people of the district. As to this proposed road, I believe it will be a saving to the Intercolonial to build it.
To the York and Carleton Railway Company for a line of railway from its present terminus westerly, not exceeding five miles.

This line runs from a point in the county of York to the St. John river. It runs in a westerly direction. The total proposed line is about 40 miles in length. The company have six miles huii.lt and running, and this will assist them to extend *it five miles.
Is this owned by a railway company ?
Yes. the York and Carleton Railway Company.
This is the one the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gibson) himself owns ?
No, I have no interest in it at all.
This is the one that is generally called
The hon. gentleman is thinking of the Canada Eastern. This is another company altogether.
Does this rnn from a point on the Canada Eastern ?
Yes, Cross Creek.
And runs to what point ?

Perth.
To the Midland Railway Company, Limited, for a line of railway from Truro northerly towards Brule, not exceeding 34 miles.

This is a line of railway, the promoters of which anticipate. I think, making Brule

the point of another crossing to Prince Edward Island.' Many years ago Brule was a point for crossing to Prince Edward Island. However, of late years other points have been used. The promoters, I think, will attempt to re-establish a line from Brule to Prince Edward Island.
For a line ot railway from' St. Peters to Louis-burg, not exceeding 50 miles.

This is a road on the south side of Cape Breton island. Hon. gentlemen who were in the House many years ago may recollect that there was what was called a battle of the routes as to which side of the island the railway should run. The government line was constructed by the central route. At the southern portion of Cape Breton island, quite a large territory, was for some years without any railway communication. Some years ago a company composed chiefly of Americans obtained a charter for a road down that coast. They have built from the Strait of Canso as far as St. Peters. The line has recently been put into operation. This will give them a right to extend the line from St. Peters down on the south side of Cape Breton island to Louisburg.
I notice that in their application they request a subsidy for bridges. Do the government propose to do anything in respect of bridges ?

The company's application covered considerably more than we are giving them, and I am afraid that can be said of a good number of applications-we have not given all they have asked. As they have now built as far as St. Peters, we have given them this grant down to Louisburg.

Is not a portion of this to be used for the construction of bridges '!
The MINISTER OB' FINANCE. No, this is for an ordinary railway appropriation.
To the Kootenay Central Railway Company for a line of railway from Golden to the international boundary line, via Windermere and Fort Steele, and crossing the Crow's Nest Railway at or near Ellso. not exceeding 106 miles.

In connection with this subsidy, I may say that the company have a charter for a line from the international boundary to Golden, which was this year extended to Fort George, on the Fraser river. That line starting at the international boundary line, crossing the Crow's nest line at Elko, passing through what is known as the Wigwain river country, a rich district of the south-east Kootenay, goes up to Fort Steele, passes along the valley of the Kootenay river through a rich mineral district where we have mines in an initial stage only waiting for transportation. It also passes through a ranching country, and a country where there are some very fair timber limits. Then it continues on from
Windermere and goes down the valley of the Columbia river to Golden, passing also through a country where we have the rich Paradise mine, and the Ptarmigan mine, both producing and shipping mines ; also through a country settled by ranchers, from the town of Golden to the town of Windermere. That will open up a district which is now entirely without railway communication, and will connect it with the Canadian Pacific Railway. In fact it will he within easy reach of the Great Northern Railway on the south, which runs now from Jennings, Montana, up to Morrisey mines, in British Columbia, also connecting with the Crow's nest line at Elko, and with the Canadian Pacific Railway line at Golden. I speak of these two mines as being in the producing stage. There are a number ol' valuable properties there only waiting for transportation facilities.
Mr. B'OWLER. Is there any lumber there V
There is lumber all along the valleys of both the Columbia and the Kootenay rivers. The Columbia Lumber Company have lumber interests all through both valleys.
Is there any portion of this built ?

None as yet. We got our Dominion charter this year. Surveys have been made over a portion of the road. The parties connected with this railway have strong financial backing in London. Mr. Pollen is one of the chief men in the transaction, the others are mostly local people, Fort Steele people. An application was made to the provincial government of British Columbia during the last sesion. The session lasted a very short time, and a number of railway subsidies that had been applied for were cut off, they did not come up. But I am told that they have reasonable assurance of aid from the provincial government.
To the Kettle River Valley Railway Company for a line of railway from Grand Forks to a point fifty miles ud the north fork and west fork of the north fork of Kettle river, not exceeding 50 miles.

This is also in my district. It is what is called the Hot Air Line. We are asking for a subsidy to continue that line further into the country. We hope to he able to make use of it in exploiting the mountains of mineral up in the North Fork district. This company, in the first place, have already built a road from Republic, in the state of Washington, crossing the boundary at Cascade, and continuing on to Grand Forks, in British territory. It is about sixty miles to Grand Forks. A portion of that is in Canadian territory. They have received no aid so far, but thev are now asking for aid to continue that line from Grand Forks up the North B'ork of the Kettle river, to the confluence

of what is known as the AVest Fork of the North Fork, and then to continue up that West Fork, in all a distance of fifty miles from Grand Forks. That also taps a rich mineral country, rich in gold, copper and silver. Further, it taps a fine coaking coal district, a necessary item in southern British Columbia for smelting purposes. They are asking for this bonus to aid in the construction of this proposed line of road for fifty miles. It is an expensive line to build.
For a line of railway from Wellington to Union Bay, not exceeding 55 miles.

That line is in the northern part of Vancouver Island. It is an extension of the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway and connects the important coal fields of Comox and the mines at Alberni on the west coast of Vancouver Island with the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway system and Victoria and Vancouver.
That line is at Wellington now.	,
Yes, the Esquimalt and Nanaimo Railway extends from Victoria and Nanaimo to Wellington and tills is an extension north.

I want to call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that just the same number of miles of road would give to the county of Colchester great satisfaction. I do not wish to oppose this item excepting in order to solicit the sympathy of the gentlemen who are pressing this item for the county of Colchester. I received a letter a few days ago from a leading Liberal in my county. The Liberals there have such confidence in me that if they want any solace they write me. The Minister of Finance will know the name of this gentleman and will communicate it to him in confidence, but as his letter is a private one I cannot mention the name publicly. This gentleman says :
I am sorry to say we are going to lose some more of our good citizens. I. B. Morrison, Mr. Finley Corbett, Silas Corbett and son leave shortly for the west, probably California. Never in the history of West Colchester has there been any such exodus and disgust that exists along the shore as has taken place in the last two years. If this thing goes on for five years more the west end of the county will contain nothing but a few old men.
Now, I do not like to read what follows, coming from a Liberal, because it is sad.
If a change of government will accomplish anything the sooner it comes the better.
That is the opinion of a very fine Liberal who is forced to say that I have no doubt, owing to the bitter fact that he has seen his neighbours leaving the country. This man lives on Cobequid bay. an arm of the Bay of Fundy which separates Cumberland from my own constituency. Formerly the coach line ran along there and all of the roads went down this bay and this was then the centre of population. People depended on Mr. GALLIHER.
the water for their transportation. When the Intercolonial Railway was built it was swung about fifteen or twenty miles to the east of these people and they soon found themselves side tracked. All the business formerly done along the shore of the bay is now done along the line of the Intercolonial Railway and the result is now as this gentleman tells me, that these people are emigrating and that in four or five years there will be nothing but old men in as fine a section of country as there is in Canada.
How far are they from a railway ?

We want a road from Truro to Parrsboro. Near Truro the Intercolonial Railway will not be more than two miles away, but as you get down eight or twelve miles from Truro it is perhaps ten miles away, and down near the shore ihe average distance would be fifteen or twenty miles. The shore country in the old days was most fertile. At a railway meeting there last year, one farmer, a very line gentleman, assured the meeting that twenty two years ago he had inherited an estate from his father which was valued by- the executors at $6,000. It is a large estate containing marsh, and it was on the through road and he said that now he could not get $2,000 for it because there was no railway near; all the trade had gone back twenty miles to the line of the Intercolonial Railway so that the property along the line of that railway which was formerly considered of no value is now worth more than his fine marsh farm. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) must be interested in this matter because when the railway gets to Parrsboro it will enter his county and ultimately be extended along the shore so as to make a continuous connection with the Intercolonial Railway. It is only fifty-five miles and is through a very level country, in fact the Intercolonial Railway was originally surveyed over this route going south of the Cobequid mountains. The interest of the iron mine at Londonderry and the Springhill mines at that time required the railway to be taken across the Cobequid mountains and as the people on the shore at that time had the water communication it was thought better to take the Intercolonial Railway over its present line ; but these people have found that the value of their property has dwindled away. I may say of the gentlemen who are referred to here that Mr. Morrison was a leading Liberal. Mr. Corbett, I think, is a Conservative. These men are middle aged, forty or fifty, and they are taking their families away from what were formerly beautiful farms. This extraordinary state of affairs exists simply because we are backward in building railways. Young people will not stay now ten or fifteen miles from a railway. They want the mails and want the brightness of the trains and they want to have travellers going through. A

railway brings brightness and lightness to a community. Owing to the absence of railways this is now almost a deserted country although it was formerly one of the finest countries in the world.
Why does not your local legislature subsidize a railway ?

The local legislature will, but I want this Dominion government to set the example and then we will force the local to follow suit. I know that the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) will agree with me that this proposal is most meritorious in every particular and one which will aid a number of lumber industries. The road will go straight past the furniture factory of which I spoke the other night as needing a light on the wharf and the whole country would then be restored to prosperity. Then if we had another short line from Brookfield to Stewiacke, thirty or forty miles, it would open up a great country. The minister will recollect that Stewiacke is in a fine country but it is to-day thirty or forty miles from a railway and the young people are leaving it. The county of Colchester, during the census decade 1S90-1900, lost over 4,000 population although it is one of the best counties in Nova Scotia. If the people will not stay In a country like that owing to the want of railways they will not stay anywhere where there are not railways. Therefore I have taken the position in this parliament that the time has come when we must have railways. The railway is the modern highway and is today as necessary to the community as the old high road was thirty or forty years ago. We must come to that view and adapt ourselves to the situation. I would ask the hon. minister to give some consideration to this Stewiacke railway. I am in the awkward position of not supporting the hon. gentleman politically and therefore I am not as much in touch with him as I should otherwise be, and I do not know that I have any other way of approaching him or if he would care to have me approach him in any other way, but I would like him to consider my application and to iisert something like reasonable subsidies. We should be liberal in these matters. Some people think that $3,200 a mile is a great temptation to build a railway. Unless the railway has an immediate commercial outlook, $3,200 is a trifling inducement and I would urge upon the minister to consider that the railways to which I have referred would serve our part of the country and would make the population there happy and contented, would induce them to stay at home and would lead to an increase in tne population and the subsidy ought to be at least doubled. That is what this country wants.
1 thank the minister for granting the subsidy for the Midland line. And I hope it will succeed in getting that railway started.
But these two railways to which I have referred are equally important, and I think 1 may say for my colleagues surrounding me, that they would have no objection if the Minister of Finance would agree to insert two subsidies for them in these resolutions. I have calculated that we will probably have $10,000,000 more next year than we had this year, giving us a total revenue of $75,000,000 or $76,000,000, and consequently we need not be penurious in these matters. These railways would be of the utmost importance to this large section of the country. They are both in the Stewiacke section and the Londonderry section, in which the stalward Liberals of the county reside. I would therefore ask the Finance Minister to include in these subsidies a double subsidy for thirty-four miles and another double subsidy for fifty-five miles, which subsidies would result in great advantage to the Dominion of Canada, because they would result in making that part of Nova Scotia happy, and contented, and cause it to enter on a career of prosperity.

I endorse what the hon. gentleman has said as to the need of a railway between Truro and Parrsboro, running from Truro through Economy and Five Islands to Parrsboro. This important part of the country is very badly in need of a railway. It is not only a long distance from any existing railway, but it is separated from that railway by a chain of mountains.
Yes; I forgot to mention that.

I do not know any part of Canada that is in more need of railway facilities than that which the hon. gentleman lias just mentioned. I endorse what he has said, and I urge upon the government the importance of providing better railway accommodation for th,e people of this section of the country. '

It is a reflection upon the agricultural capabilities of Nova Scotia, to say that men will leave that province because they have not a railway within ten or twelve miles of them. How did we settle the province of Manitoba and the prairies, when the people had to carry their wheat seventy and eighty miles to a railway station ? It is not until within the last four or five years, when the province of Manitoba itself bonused roads, that the majority of settlers have been able to get a railway within ten or twelve miles of them. Yet here is the province of Nova Scotia, settled for a hundred years before Manitoba was known, and it comes to the Dominion and asks for subsidies when the inhabitants already have railways not more than ten or twelve miles away. I was told by one of the ministers this session, that the reason why there were such large grants to the maritime provinces for wharfs and breakwaters. was because the means of locomo-

1449(1
tion in the maritime provinces was by water. Now I see that they come here and ask us for large grants for railways as well. In the province of Manitoba, which is to-day yielding more revenue to the Dominion of Canada than any other province in confederation per head of population-
No.
I am making the statement, and I know what I am saying. Take our bank returns, post office returns, inland revenue returns, customs returns, and they are ahead of any other province per capita.
Except British Columbia.
We exceed British Columbia by $100,000, according to population.
No you don't.

I will leave it to the Minister of Customs, the Minister of Inland Revenue or the Postmaster General. Our post office revenue to-day is nearly as much as for the .entire province of British Columbia.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh.

I know what I am saying, and notwithstanding that, all that is voted for the province of Manitoba here is practically thirty-six miles of railway. I will ask the minister next year to seriously consider relieving the province of Manitoba from the large obligations which they have undertaken to build railways. If they do it for other provinces, there is no reason why they should not do it for Manitoba.
How many miles of railway did you say were subsidized in Manitoba this year ?
Thirty-six.
Look at the list and you will find 139 miles.
You are talking: about the Territories. There are only 36 miles for Manitoba, and that is a re-vote.
You can scarcely throw a stone in the province of Manitoba without hitting a railway.
We built them ourselves.
I will guarantee that my hon. friend from Colchester and myself will be perfectly satisfied if we get one-quarter the railways in Nova Scotia that you have in Manitoba.

I desire to correct my hon. friend (Mr. McCreary) and to state that the province of British Columbia contributes more money to the Dominion treasury per capita than does any other province in the Dominion of Canada.
For a line of railway from Midway to Vernon, not exceeding 150 miles.

This railway runs from Midway in the Boundary country ; or rather the charter is from Midway to the town of Vernon. It starts from Midway, goes up the west fork of the Kettle river, thence east of the Okanagan lake to the Okanagan falls, five miles from Vernon, where it will join with what is now known as the Shuswap and Okanagan road, running from that point to join the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway at Sicamous Junction. That will connect the great farming, ranching, and fruit growing district of the Okanagan around Vernon, Armstrong, Kelowna, En-derby, Peachland and White 'Valley, with the mineral districts of the south, thus affording these districts access to their natural market. The government could not possibly give a subsidy which will produce better results, than this very subsidy under consideration.
Is there any company ready to undertake this work ?
Oh, yes ; the Midway and Vernon Railway Company have applied for this.
They have not built yet ?

No. I may state that there is a provincial subsidy for this line amounting to $4,500 per mile, payable in provincial bonds.
To the St. Mary's River Railway Company for a line of railway from Spring Coulee, crossing St. Mary's river to Cardston, sixteen miles, and from a point on this line to or near the intake of the Irrigation canal, about sixteen miles, in all not exceeding 32 miles. Total, 48.

This is what is known as the Galt road.
, Mr. HUGHES (Victoria). Did they get a charter this year ?

No, they have built a considerable portion of the road. This country is being settled up a great deal and splendid results have followed the irrigation works established by the company. I am satisfied that this road is worthy of every assistance we can give it.
1 do not quite understand about mileage here. In the margin it says forty-eight miles, but in the resolution it says : In all not exceeding thirty-two miles.

I think there is an error there. We will make it thirty-two miles.
Resolution, as amended, agreed to.
For a lime of railway from Dawson city to Stewart river, passing at or near Grand Forks, not exceeding 84 miles.
This is a proposal to build a road as described in the

item. Application is made on behalf of the Klondike Mines Railway Company, by its solicitor at Ottawa. I understand that it is a very substantial company. This road, if constructed, will be the most northern road on the continent of America. 1 think we are all anxious to develop the Yukon country, and if we can give the people internal railway communication, even though we have not yet a connection with the Yukon, I think it will be very desirable.
What is the object of the road ?
It is a general railway to provide communication between different sections there.

In view of the fact that Canada has no entrance to the Yukon and no port to the Yukon on the Pacific ocean, are the government taking into their serious consideration the advisability of building a railway to the Yukon through Canadian territory ? I wanted the Prime Minister a year ago to pledge himself that he would build a road from Kitimat Arm.

We will have to do that now since the award.
To the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for a branch line from a point on the main line between Moosomin and Elkhorn, north-westerly to a point in the neighbourhood of the Pheasant Hills, not exceeding 136 miles.
I am going to ask the minister if he will let this item stand. I fear there are some questions which I shall have to ask concerning the proposal.
The hon. gentleman will have a chance later on when the Bill is in committee.
I would like to ask the minister who is the applicant for this ?
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

Like my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) last night, I am to a considerable degree surprised to hear that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has been an applicant for a subsidy, in view of the fact that we have been told by a prominent director of that company in recent years that it opposes the principle of parliament granting railway subsidies. Was the company the only applicant ?
For this particular road, yes.

I am not satisfied that this item should be adopted. Yesterday evening the hon. Postmaster General gave a piece of very god advice to the House. He said that if any hon. member objected to the policy of subsidies in general or to any particular subsidy in particular, be should move against it, and I fear that it will be necessary for 454
me to make such a motion in regard to this particular proposition, which I am bound to say does not meet with my approval. I am not opposed in general to the policy of granting subsidies ; but there are certain conditions which I think are necessary to make the granting of subsidies justifiable. I am willing In all cases to vote for proper and reasonable assistance for railways in districts where people require railway ac: cominodation and cannot obtain it in any Other way. My information concerning this particular proposition may not be full or precisely accurate ; but my impression is that the greater part of the line for which this subsidy is proposed to be voted is already constructed. This is for a branch line of the Canadian Pacific Railway commencing at a point called Kirkella between Elk-horn and Moosomin, just on the boundary line between Manitoba and Assiniboia, which runs northwesterly from the main line of the Pacific. The construction of the road was commenced eighteen or nineteen months ago, and my impression is that practically the whole of the 136 miles mentioned here have been graded and nearly 100 miles have been ironed. My recollection also is that we have been told in the Railway Committee on more than one occasion by representatives of the company that this particular line was being constructed without any aid and that they did not propose to ask for aid.
Was the charter for that road applied for during the present session ?
No.
Then it surely did not come up during the present session.

This particular road has been mentioned in connection with other charters applied for by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and by other companies, and my recollection is that the representatives of the company stated on more than one occasion that this road was being built without any aid. It does seem to me a strange proposition to grant a subsidy to procure the construction of a road for the benefit of the people when in fact the road is already constructed. It does not seem to be necessary to aid it ; and, with my present information, I am bound to say that this proposition does not appeal to me as being a proper one.
Has not the bon. gentleman voted for several schemes of the same kind ?
Not to my knowledge.

When I am supporting a subsidy, speaking for myself, I do not take into consideration so much the company which is to be benefited as the interest of the public in the section of country which is to be served by the railway. I do not think we should



lay too much stress on statements male by individuals in the course of their arguments In the Railway Committee or even in this House ; because they have no authority to speak for the company or for the public in that particular district. No member of this House, I suppose, is particularly anxious to grant a subsidy to any railway company, even the Canadian Pacific Railway; but some years ago there was a great demand by the settlers in this district for further railway accommodation. As the House well knows, no subsidies were granted a year ago, and when the people of this district were asking for further railway facilities, they were probably told that they would receive the same consideration from parliament and the same recommendation from the government as other sections of the country where the government felt that further railway facilities should be provided. They proceeded with the construction of this road, believing that they would receive the same treatment as any other responsible company, the road is opening up a good district of country, and i do not think my hon. friend should press his objection.

I take it that this railway is to run through the constituency of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). When he reads ' Hansard,' the hon. gentleman will find that the remarks he has made with regard to it were very guarded. If he will subtract what he thinks and his impressions and recollections, there will be very little left. Before he attempts to furnish us with information, he should be more definite and state the actual facts. I do not think it is any argument that because a director of any company is opposed to subsidies, we should not give his company a subsidy to which it is entitled. One of the directors may be opposed to subsidies and the others may be in favour of it, and the public also, and we must not consider simply the one dissenting director. The hon. gentleman to whom the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) referred, is not present. He may have no personal knowledge of this subsidy or anything in connection with it, and it is hardly fair to make his presumed dissent a reason for opposing the. grant, if it be a deserving one.
Am I to understand that the railway is already built ?

It is a matter of common knowledge that its construction was begun in the early part of last year. My information is that the line for this distance is all graded, and that the greater portion of it is already ironed. In fact the people in the districts along this route were assured a year ago that the line would, by the end of this fall, be constructed to a much greater distance than these 136 miles. Hon. members must recollect that this particular Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
line was the subject of very considerable discussion in yearS gone by. Two years ago it occupied a considerable portion of the time of this House. Three years ago a contract or agreement was entered into by the company to build year by year a certain portion-twenty-one miles, if not more, it appears to me that the fact that such an agreement was entered into without any stipulation that aid should be granted in the way of a subsidy, ought to weigh very considerably with this committee. The idea that aid is to be granted for the construction of this road will be a matter of very great surprise to everybody in the district. Three or four years ago, when the people had been waiting for years ajid appealing for years to the government and the Canadian Pacific Railway to take some steps which would secure the building of this line, the proposition to grant it a subsidy would then have been understood, but the appeals of the people did not have much weight with the Canadian Pacific Railway and the government until now. After more encouragement in the way of business, I suppose, had been offered to the company, they decided over a year ago to begin the construction of this railway, and this particular mileage has been, to all intents and purposes, completed. To the people along the route, it will be a matter of very great surprise to learn that parliament, at this late day, determines to grant aid to a proposition which is practically completed. If the proposition were to grant aid to 136 miles of road from Pheasant Hills westward, and thus give railway facilities to communities which are still without the means of transportation, it would be one we could understand, but no reason has been advanced yet which leads me to consider that the proposition before us is in any sense justifiable.

It is quite true that this railway was commenced last year and is nearly completed. It would have been subsidized last year, but no subsidies were then granted, and the company went on in the expectation of getting a subsidy as soon as subsidies would be granted.

Had the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott), when we heard the resolution to subsidize a road going through the St. John district, given attention to what was going on, he would have seen that the committee regarded the fact tl\at the road was under construction as rather a favourable indication that the project would be carried out, and were all the more disposed to grant the subsidy. I know nothing about the merits of the road in question, but the best security which the country can have that the promoters are in earnest, when asking for a subsidy, is the fact that they committee regarded the fact that the road will open up a new district to colonization, and is deserving of a subsidy, the fact that

it is partially or wholly constructed does not detract from its claim.

I might remind the hon. gentleman from Assiniboia that we have granted a subsidy to a short line of railway
which was completed last spring.

From my personal knowledge of the people living out along this line, this road is very much needed. We have been trying to get a road built through that district for the last twenty years. Twice a portion of that road has been built, but somehow or other the company burst up, and the enterprise failed. There are many farmers, with whom I am well acquainted, who went out there some sixteen or twenty years ago, and who, up to last fall, have been without any railway convenience, and I do think, from my knowledge of the country, that this railway will certainly be of great advantage to the people and is deserving of aid.

In view of the chorus of disapproval which came from the opposite side last evening in general against the policy of granting subsidies to railway companies, it is rather surprising that when an hon. gentleman gets up and submits practical objections against some particular item, he is greeted from the other side with a chorus of commendation of the whole policy of granting subsidies and especially of the particular item under consideration. I feel impelled to accept the advice given by the Postmaster General last evening. This proposition is not one which I can conscientiously support, and I beg to move that this item be struck out.
Amendment negatived.

The only thing I see to criticise in this subsidy is that the road runs from a point between Moosomin and Elkhorn. Why not say Kirkella Y The railway is necessary, and I do not object to the bonus. In fact, I think it is a very proper and necessary road to assist. But I do not like this coming down and deceiving the committee. The road starts from Kirkella.
I think that is what it means.
Then why not say so ? The road is already built. We all know that. '

1 enter my protest against this vote. I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). This road, I understand, is built through an important part of the western country. I believe that it will pay its running expenses and interest upon the investment. It has already been built without subsidy or promise of a subsidy. And yet this House, in its generosity, proposes to grant a subsidy for 136 miles through a country so rich and of such promise that the 454J
company has begun the work and practically completed it before even asking for a subsidy. We do not it seems confine ourselves to granting subsidies to encourage the building of roads, but we grant subsidies for roads already built. I am sorry the motion of the hon. member for West Assiniboia did not carry, for it seems plain to me that this subsidy should not be granted.

Here is an opportunity for the government to control rates under an actual agreement, not the visionary control of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, or the still more visionary control of this less effective and far more corruptible body, the proposed commission, but a genuine control under agreement. I do not agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) who sits beside me. I believe this bonus should be given, but I believe also that some control of rates should go with it. I happened to have an instance of what can be done brought before me the other day. A young man came from the North-west who was proposing to open a route to connect with the Pasqua branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway in Dakota. A part of the route would be covered by steamer transportation on a long lake that crosses the boundary. It was estimated that it would cost only three cents a bushel to bring the grain from the district to be served by this route to the Pasqua branch. At present they have to haul the grain twenty miles to the Canadian Pacific Railway. By the new route they figured they would save from four cents to seven, cents a bushel. The matter was brought before the Minister of Customs, and it was decided that it would not be possible to allow the arrangement. But it was pointed out that if the farmers in that district gave the seven cents per bushel that they would save on three season's crop, they could build a road to connect with the Canadian Pacific Railway. Now, this road that we are bonus-ing runs through a farming section, and I take it to be the government's business to see to it that the farmers of that country get the benefit of this $3,200 a mile that we vote ; and the way to secure that benefit for them is to properly regulate the rates. If that is not done, what is the use of voting this money ? If the farmers pay as high rates as ever, we might as well withhold our assistance. Every road that receives a subsidy should have its rates controlled, not, as I say, by this visionary organization, the railway commission, or by the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, but by a hard and fast agreement under the Bill.
