I see that section 6 of these resolutions provides that ' the Governor in Council shall have absolute control at all times over the rates and tolls to oe levied and taken by any of the companies, or by any of the railways, hereby subsidized.'
The Governor in Council doesn't amount to a hill of beans, so far as the controlling of these rates is concerned.
I am afraid the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) is not loyal to the Crown.

Not if the Crown is supposed to mean the Prime Minister and the fellows behind him, who are pulling on all sides. The Mackenzie & Mann road, the Canadian Northern, affords an illustration of what I want. They have an agreement with the Manitoba government that the rates shall be controlled thus and so. The people are behind the agreement, and no matter how much the government might like to please the railway company by allowing the rates to remain high, the voice of the people controls and the law has to be observed.
This is the law also, and the voice of the people is behind it.
The right hon. Prime Minister knows well that the moment you mention ' Governor in Council ' the people bow. They demand nothing ; they are afraid.
The people, including Colonel Hughes ?
I am only one of the people, and I am not in the Northwest.

As the House is apparently unanimous in favour of this grant, it may be superfluous for me to say anything further. But I feel that notwithstanding that my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) did not give me any support, I ought to support his contention in this case. This session a very considerable amount of ai'd was granted to another company, the Canadian Northern, to extend their present line to Prince Albert and Edmonton, and a hard and fast contract was demanded of that company, was forced upon them, providing that they should haul North-west wheat on a ten-cent basis from Winnipeg to the lakes. It seems to me it is not fair to make fowl of one company and flesh of another. If it is fair to compel the Canadian Northern to give a contract for maximum rates, then aid granted to this other company should carry with it a similar condition. In this case we should make a contract with the company with regard to the rates to be charged to the people in the district.
For a line of railway from a point at or near Medicine Hat on the Canadian Pacific Railway to the coal fields in or near townships 12 and 13, range 6. west of fourth principal meridian, not exceeding eight miles.
Let us have an explanation of this.

This is an item which I think is entirely justifiable. The aid is being granted to a road from the town of Medicine Hat, in a southwesterly direction, to the coal fields about eight miles distant from the town. A land grant was voted for this road some years ago, but that has been cancelled.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) should know more about it than I do. But I thought this road ran northerly, that it was part of the old road intended to run to Buffalo lake and up to the coal lands. But the exact direction is immaterial. The road will open up large coal mines near Medicine Hat, the opening of which is very necessary for the people of that community.
Might I ask in what direction the road is to run ? Does it run north or south ?
The material point is that it runs to the coal fields.
This is opening up a new policy entirely. Is it the policy of the government to grant bonuses for the purpose of extending railways to coal fields ?

It is not wise to adopt general policies in these things. This case may be taken on its merits. But the extension of railways to coal fields would not be a bad idea if it were made a general principle.
The coal mines are in townships 12 and 13, range (S, north of Medicine Hat, down the river.
My hon. friend is mistaken about this. I am perfectly certain that the road runs in a southwesterly direction.

The minister says it might be a good policy for the government to adopt. I would like to draw attention to the fact that the press of Canada has been calling upon the government of the Dominion, as well as upon the territorial and provincial governments, to assist in building lines that will enable the people to procure fuel, which is not plentiful In that western country. I agree with the hon. gentleman when he says that it is an important thing to assist railways to these coal mines, because it is a well known fact that large portions of that new territory [DOT] are so thinly populated that it would not pay a railway company to build a line to these coal fields without public assistance. I trust the government will take that matter into consideration, because it is in the interests of the people who are being sent in there. They have little or no wood, with which the people in the older provinces are well supplied. I believe the coal in the territories is well adapted for domestic use, but the mines are situated at a great distance from the railways.
To the Lake Superior, Long Lake and Albany Railway Company for a line of railway from Peninsula harbour in a northerly direction, not exceeding 10 miles.

This is opening up a new district from Peninsula harbour, on Lake Superior, in a northerly direction. The provincial government, at its last session, granted a subsidy of $3,000 a mile for 10 miles. The road is chartered to run to Albany river north.
Who makes the application ?
The application is signed by John W. Cheesewood, of Toronto. This gentleman signs himself on behalf of the syndicate.
He is the solicitor for the company.
Does the Minister of Public Works know who is the moving spirit ?

No. I am not sure whether the solicitor was introduced to me when these representations were made. A memorandum was given to me of the Act of incorporation, and of the grant by the provincial government.
I know Mr. Cheesewood to meet him. I did not ask him who the directors of the company were. It is quite a large undertaking. and the provincial government thought it of sufficient importance in that new country to grant $3,000 a mile for 10 miles, and we duplicate the grant. I may say with regard to the great majority, if not all, the subsidies that are granted in Ontario, that we have been guided a great deal by the representations made by the municipalities and the provincial authorities. I do not believe there is a single subsidy granted that is not made to supplement a grant made by municipalities or by the provincial government. The people in the various localities who are more directly in touch with the local authorities, have succeeded in convincing them of the necessity and importance of these works, and we have thought well to be guided by that fact in supplementing local aid with Dominion subsidies. We have, therefore, good assurance that the railways will be proceeded with. I have no knowledge personally of tbe incorporators of this company, nor have any records been submitted to me.

I think the government ! may be congratulated upon having shown a disposition to colonize northern Ontario. This is the fifth or sixth line that has been granted a subsidy all leading from tbe Canadian Pacific Railway north into that country. They will all act as feeders for tbe Canadian Pacific Railway, and will all offer facilities for the colonization of that country, and for taking out the pulp wood and other timber products. We have the satisfaction of knowing at least that full provision has been made both for colonization and other railways in that country. I shall repeat what I said last night, that we have no longer any fear of that country not being abundantly supplied with railways for settlement and general trade, and there will now be no hurry for the line between Quebec and Winnipeg for the purposes of colonization. This is a very satisfactory feature, even at the close of the session, and it is a very great pity that this had not been considered before hon. gentlemen entered upon that unfortunate enterprise of constructing the road, where they are constructing it, from Quebec to Winnipeg.
. To the Cumberland Railway and Coal Company for a line of railway from Parrsboro' station to Riverside wharf, not exceeding one mile.

This is to furnish a link between the water and rail communication at this point. The boat from Wolville on the other side of the bay lands at tbe government wharf. The Spring Hill and Parrsboro road ends at the private wharf of the company abou.t a mile away, so that passengers have to walk that distance and it is thought advisable to avoid that interruption.

This will accommodate the coal company.
The MINISTER' OF FINANCE. No, this will accommodate the travelling public ; the coal company would be quite content to have our people walk down a mile from the railway to the wharf.
I suppose this will include the whole cost ?
Oh, no, $3,000 will not build a mile of railway any where in Canada.
This is a first class railway and I think from what I know of it that it is essential from the public standpoint.

This mile of railway is not a part of the National Transcontinental Railway but it is very important to Parrsboro which is a town of three thousand inhabitants. At present the railway from Springhill to Parrsboro does not run nearer than a mile to the public wharf, and all goods have to he trucked from that wharf a mile to the station at Parrsboro. The purpose of this is to have the road carried to the wharf so that goods will no longer have to be trucked.

Here is a case of a wharf being built by the public and then to avoid the expense of hauling the goods for one mile the country is expected to build a railway for these people for that distance. I think, as I said before, that the government has gone mad on subsidizing railways. This is not in any sense a colonization road

and it is most absurd. If the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce were litre his heart would go faint and sick to see a vote of this kind.

I would draw attention to the fact that this is a parallel case to the one I mentioned before, the case of Meaford, where the people of the town had to raise $25,000 of their own money to build a railway two miles to their wharf.

The coal company run a railway down to Parrsboro and that ia all they want ; they do not care for anything else. There is a mile between the terminus of that road and the shore of Minas Basin. The steamer goes there with passengers and the passengers have to walk one mile.
Does this company not ship coal by this wharf ?

Not by the public wharf; they have a private wharf. I think it is demeaning to the province that strangers and tourists should have to walk a mile. The company have no object in building this railway, it is purely in the interest of the public.

It makes the case exactly parallel with the case I mentioned in Meaford, in which the government refused to grant any aid.
To the Indian River Railway Company for a line of railway from a point at or near the north end of Lake Megantic, thence southerly along said lake to a point on the international boundary. not exceeding 19 miles.
The description of this in the vote gives about as much information as any one can give about it, describing the points between which it will run.

This road is intended to connect the Quebec Central Railway at the end of its Tring branch on Lake Megantic with the boundary line, at Rangeley with a railway that goes up from Rumford. This little extension to the State of Maine will enable the farmers in that district to communicate with the lumber camps in the State of Maine. It practically affords a straight line for the Quebec Central Railway into the United States.
This is an independent company is it not ?

Yes, it connects the Quebec Central with this company at Rangeley.
Towards the construction and completion of a railway bridge and approaches over the Nicolet river at Nicolet, in lieu of a grant under chapter 8 of 63-64 Victoria, item 39 of section 2, $15,000.
This is a revote of a subsidy which was granted in 1900, for the South Shore Railway bridge on the Nicolet river.
What has this bridge cost ?
In tbe neighbourhood of $100,000.

I suggested the other day that it would be a great advantage if these railway bridges were so constructed that they could be used for passenger and vehicular traffic. In all the bridges over tbe Mississippi river, they are so constructed that they can be used by the general public as well as by railways.
Hear, hear.
That cannot be done in this case, because tbe piers have already been constructed, and it has not been provided for.
speakername: The MINISTER OE MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Heretofore the principle lias been laid down, that the government would grant about 15 per cent of the cost of these bridges. On what principle are we proceeding here ?

The principle is that we generally give 15 per cent except when bridges are very expensive, and in such a case the subsidy is calculated on tbe cost of the bridge, and is an arbitrary one.
Towards the construction of the steel superstructure of a railway bridge on the St. Francis river, in the county of Yamaska, in lieu of a grant under chapter 8 of 63-64 Victoria, item 38 of section 2, hut subject to the same conditions as expressed therein, payable to Canadian Bridge Company of Walkervi'lle, as their claim may appear for work already done on said bridge, $50,000.

This subsidy was voted three years ago, and a contract was entered into between the South Shore Railway Company, and the Canadian Bridge Company of Walkerville, for the steel superstructure. The superstructure is there today, but there are no approaches to the bridge. Th,e bridge will be of no use to anybody unless it is completed. We ask parliament simply to revote tbe item, so that the bridge company can receive its money.
We have not given them any money at all ?
They have received no money yet.
In this resolution you speak of the superstructure only, and in the other resolution you speak of the bridge as a whole. What is the distinction ?
The Walkerville Bridge Company will receive $48,000 and the other $2,000 will be to pay some claims against tbe bridge.
Then you ar,e voting this to tbe bridge company, and not to the railway company ?
We are voting it to pay the bridge company, because they are really the parties entitled to it.
How much has this bridge cost ?
I do not know what the masonry cost ; but the bridge must have cost considerably more than $100,000.
If it cost $100,000 we are giving 50 per cent.
I am sure that it cost more than $100,000.

I am safe in saying that it will cost over $200,000. It is a two-story bridge, providing for vehicles and passengers, as well as the railway, and it can be used by the municipalities on both sides of the river.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Is it free to the public ?
The Minister of marine and FISHERIES. Yes.
Does this pay all the charges which the bridge company has against the bridge ?
Yes, except as is provided in the next resolution.
Did the provincial government give any assistance to this bridge ?
Yes, the provincial government has given so much a year for ten or fifteen years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: It is only proper that the provincial government should aid such a bridge, especially as it affords facilities for the travelling public.
I understand that this money will not be earned until all the work is done.
It is not the intention to pay until the approaches have been completed.
It is very proper that the Walkerville Bridge Company should be paid for the superstructure, but have we any assurance that the balance of the work will be done ?

That is exactly what w,e provide for in the next resolution.
To the Canadian Bridge Company of Walker-ville. To strengthen and complete the foundation and approaches to the bridge over the St. Francis river subsidized to the South Shore Railway Company by section 3, chapter 7, Victoria 62-63. a sum of $35,000, which amount shall remain the first Charge on the road, and to be recouped to the treasury out of subsidies earned or to be earned, $35,000.

As I have just stated that the Walkerville Bridge Company have put up the superstructure, hut the
bridge is in the river without any approaches. The railway company is insolvent, and we thought we should take some precaution to have the bridge completed, so that the public could have the benefit of it. We agreed with the Walkerville company to give them a subsidy of $25,000. First of all we provide that they shall strengthen the piers. Our engineers have reported that the piers would have to be strengthened, so as to provide against the ice. We then provided that for this amount of $25,000 they should complete the approaches. When they have built the approaches and strengthened the piers, then they will be paid the $25,000, and the $48,000 which is due for the superstructure.
Who is In possession of this road ?
The railway company is still in possession of the road, but they are insolvent.
The railway has . not reached there.
It has.
They have ten miles graded on the other side.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: We have provided this sum of money not as an extra subsidy but as a charge on the road to be recouped by the government.
1 do not quite understand how this is to he returned by way of earned subsidy.

I have just explained that the railway is completed to the bridge. There are between four and six miles of the railway for which the subsidy has been earned, but not paid, so that we have nearly $20,000 which we can apply to recoup ourselves for the further subsidy which we are giving for the completion of the bridge.
I understood that this bridge would cost over $100,000. We are giving $85,000 to build a bridge which is to cost a little over $100,000.

We do not give $85,000. We give $50,000, and we advance $115,000, which is to be recouped.
To Uie Chateauguay and Northern Railway Company. In' addition) to the subsidy for the Bout de L/Tle 'bridge granted by chapter 8, section 33, Victoria 63-64, $50,000.

This bridge was also subsidized two years ago. It is now in process of construction, and is partly built, but it turns out to be far more expensive than was supposed. It was estimated to cost between $500,000 and $600,000. The report we have is that It will cost probably $700,000. The condition of the country has

been found to be such as to make it much more expensive, and the plans had to be changed.
What bridge is this ?
It is at the eastern extremity of the Island of Montreal, connecting it with the main land on the north side, crossing the two branches of the Ottawa river.
What was the subsidy two years ago ?

One hundred and eighty thousand dollars.
To the Tilsoniburg, Lake Erie and Pacific Railway Company for a line of railway from Woodstock northerly to a point on the Grand Trunk Railway at Berlin, or from Ingersoll to Stratford. or to any point on the Grand Trunk Railway between these places, not exceeding 35 miles, being in addition to, and continuation of the nine miles mentioned in Item one of this section. [DOT]

This item was allowed to stand at the request of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule). I telegraphed to the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton), and he says that the wording here was adopted after full consideration by the directors of the company, and he does not like to authorize a change. I have consulted the hon. member for East Grey, and I believe it will meet the views of the committee to allow it to pass if the bon. gentleman will withdraw his amendment.
Amendment of Mr. Sproule withdrawn, and item agreed to.
On resolution 4,
The subsidies hereby authorized towards the construction of any railway or bridge shall be payable out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, and may, unless otherwise expressly provided in this Act, at the option of the Governor in Council, on the-report of the Minister of Railways and Canals, be paid as follows :- (a.) upon the completion of the work subsidized ; or
(b.) by Instalments, on the completion of each ten-mile section of the railway, in the proportion which the cost of such completed section bears to that of the whole work undertaken ; or (c.) upon the progress estimates on the certificate of the chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals, that, in his opinion, having regard to the whole work undertaken and the aid granted, the progress made justifies the payment of a sum not less than sixty thousand dollars ; or
(d.) with respect to (b) and (c), part one way, part the other.

I move that this resolution be amended by substituting in subsection 0. $30,000 for $60,000. The object is to make the subsection correspond with the Act adopted this session. $60,000 would apply in the case of large enterprises, but in the case of a shorter road it would be a very large sum. There Sir WILFRIP LAURIER.
are times when you cannot certify that the road is completed, but the general progress made gives such assurance of completion that it would be quite legitimate to make payment on a progress estimate.

With regard to the resolution we have just passed, resolution No. 3, relating to bridges, the hon. minister is aware no doubt that a dispute arose between the Auditor General and some company with regard to the cost of a bridge. Has the government made any additional provision for ascertaining accurately what the cost of any bridge is, because when we are paying a percentage the cost may be made out greater than it really is. That is what happened in the case I referred to.
We could not put any legislation on the statute-book which would broaden the powers of the government in this respect. That is a matter for inquiry by the engineers.
Have you adopted any additional safeguards in these resolutions than are to be found in the others ?

The resolutions are the same, but in the light of experience the department will adopt additional safeguards where the necessity arises. There is no legislation required to broaden the powers of the department.

It was suggested that there was a defect in the regulations or in the carrying out of them. When the attention of the government is drawn to it, 1 should think they would he more careful in the future.

The powers of the government seem to be sufficiently broad. The only thing that might be suggested is that parliament might impose a specific mode of inquiry on the officers of the department before they could act on the provisions of section 3. That may or may not be necessary, and I do not offer any opinion with regard to it. I do not know whether or not there is in these resolutions any provision to ensure the operation of the railway after it is constructed. I do not know that it is very easy to insert such a provision but i1s necessity was brought to the attention of the government this session by the fact that two railways which had received aid from this government and the provincial government, had not been in operation for several months, and one of them is not in operation yet. Under section 4 of these resolutions, a railway company may procure its subsidy in very small amounts from time to time, and there does not seem to be any stipulation which will ensure the final completion of the road. I do not know whether the form of contract and the safeguards therein provided give any assurance that a road, after receiving subsidies over a certain mileage, will be really completed. It is desirable that the

country should have some assurance that any road which receives the assistance of the government should be operated after completion. The ex-Miuister of Railways said at the time it was a matter for serious consideration but he did not know of any measure which could be adopted that would aid us in that regard. Has the subject received the consideration of the government, because it seems closely connected with the provisions of section 4 ?

The matter has received some consideration. Although the statute does not deal with the matter particularly, the practice of the department has been to insert a clause in all the contracts, requiring the company to operate the road. Still while that clause is there, we have not always found it possible to discover the means of enforcing it. 1 have referred the form of contract to the Justice Department to see whether we cannot strengthen the clause in any way, and I am awaiting its opinion.

It seems that there is a very lax method of paying out the subsidies on bridges. They may be paid out on pro-' gress estimates, certified to by the chief engineer. This section provides that payment may be made of a sum not less than $30,000, but it does not say that this payment shall bear any proportion to the cost of the work.
The engineer will see to that.
I think he will be more likely to attend to it if he has something to guide him.
The section says ' having regard to the whole work undertaken and the aid granted.' That means a proportionate sum.
If they had $30,000 worth of work done in the judgment of the engineer, he would be justified in certifying to the progress estimates to that extent.
That is not done. The practice is exactly what my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) wishes. It must be a reasonable proportion of the whole work.
No proposition is stated here.

No, the engineer must be satisfied that it is a reasonable proportion of the whole work.
On section 5,
The subsidies hereinbefore authorized to be granted to companies named shall, if granted by the Governor in Council, be granted to such companies respectively ; the other subsidies may he granted to such companies as establish to the satisfaction of the Governor in1 Council their ability to construct and complete the said railways respectively ; all the lines for the construction of which subsidies are granted, unless they are already commenced, shall he commenced within two years from the first day of August, 1903, and completed within a reasonable time, not to exceed four years from the said first day of August, to be fixed by the Governor in Council, and shall also be constructed according to desc-riptionis, conditions and specifications approved by the Governor in Council on the report of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and specified in each case in a contract between the company and the said minister, which contract the minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council, is hereby empowered to make. The location also of such subsidized lines shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.

How is that carried out in practice ? Is any notice given to persons or communities interested ? Complaint has been made to me during the present session of unfair location of railway lines which are receiving aid from the government, and it is said that this is done without any notice whatever to the municipal body or to the people of a community where there is no municipal organization.

Complaint is likely to arise in matters of this kind where there are conflicting interests. But I have not had my attention called to any grievance as to lack of notice. My own observation is that wherever a road is being surveyed a very lively interest is taken in the location of the line, and if all parties are not satisfied, complaint is likely to he made. There is no special rule as to notifying any of the parties concerned, but, as I say, I do not think there is any grievance arising out of that lack of notice.

I refer to cases of this kind : Suppose a town situated practically upon the proposed line of railway, and the railway located in such a way that instead of running to the town, it runs at a distance of two or three miles, the result being that the property of persons in the town is much less valuable than it would otherwise be. In such a case the tendency is gradually to transfer the town to a point near the line of railway, and the people owning property in the town, rightly or wrongly, feel aggrieved. It may be that, in such cases, there is good reason for locating the line of railway as it is located ; I am not discussing that, but I am discussing the allegation which is said to be literally true, that lines are located in that way without notice to the municipal governments or the people of the town. Whatever may he said as to the merits of any particular case, the people of the town should be notified before the location is fixed by the government. I do not know whether the facts are as represented to me ; I am asking for information.

If the line were first located so as to run to a town and before construction the proposal were made to change it, that is a thing, it seems

to me, that would interfere with vested rights on which the people should be heard. But where you are dealing with the first location the case would hardly be the same. But I think that, so far as notice is concerned, the first appearance of a surveyor in the region attracts attention and arouses interest, and if the location fails to meet the wishes of the community generally, we find that representations are very promptly and freely made through various channels. But I have never had any complaint made of lack of information.
On section 6,
The granting of such subsidies, and the receipt thereof by the respective companies, shall be subject to the condition that the Governor in Council may at all times provide and secure to other companies such running powers, traffic arrangements and other rights, as will afford to all railways connecting with those so subsidized, reasonable and proper facilities in exercising such running powers, fair and reasonable traffic arrangements with connecting companies, and equal mileage rates between all such connecting railways ; and the Governor in Council shall have absolute control, at all times, over the rates and tolls to he levied and taken by any of the companies, or upon any of the railways hereby subsidized.

I observe that the Governor in Council is given control over rates. Is that intended to be in contradistinction to the powers to be exercised by tbe new Railway Commission? It strikes me that there Is something a little inconsistent in this; at all events, we should have some definition as to when the rates are to be fixed by tbe Railway Commission and when by the Governor in Council.

We have followed the phraseology of the old Act In this respect, and I am inclined to think that before this Bill is finally passed we shall have to adapt it to the provisions of the Railway Commission Act.

I notice that the expression * Governor in Council ' is used throughout these resolutions. In some cases, no doubt, it is tbe proper expression, but in other cases it may be necessary to make an amendment.

It may be that, in following the wording of the old Act, we have not made the changes made necessary by the new. Before tbe Bill is finally disposed of, I shall see to it that that shall be looked into.

Another point relates to the terms of the proposed covenant to be inserted in the contract, which is to be in addition to, or in substitution of, the powers conferred upon the Railway Commission. It seems to me that such matters are pretty well covered by the terms of the Railway Act passed during the present session. I do not say that it would be wrong to insert them in this Bill as well, but we should see Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
to it that tbe language with regard to running powers, traffic arrangements, &e., is made absolutely to conform with tbe provisions of the Railway Act. And very probably it will be found that the Railway Act, having been altered in some respect, and this Bill having been founded on the former Act, the language is not exactly in conformity with the new law.

I agree that the terms should correspond exactly with those of the Railway Act unless we find something to add. In this case, it may be agreed that, while we can take the exact provisions of the Railway Act, there is advantage sometimes in making them a matter of contract. They would Tie, in a sense, a matter of contract under the conditions of the statute. But sometimes it is an advantage to have them under the hand and seal of tbe company, as then the company is not in a position to contest them. At any rate, tbe language should conform to that of the Railway Act.

Of course, a company may have successors, but I never knew it could have assigns, as we find in this section. Is there not a provision in an Act passed during the present session witli regard to some matters dealt with in this section ?
I think this section is covered by the Railway Act.
Would there be any objection to an amendment or an additional clause by which the Auditor General could also have a perusal of the books of the company during construction ?
I do not think any practical difficulty could arise there.
There was the case of the bridge, where the Auditor General said the bridge did not cost the amount that was claimed, and he saved the country a considerable sum of money.

There is no difficulty in the Auditor General getting

all the information he desires. He employed experts in the particular case referred to, and there is no difficulty under the statutes in the Auditor General getting all the information he wishes.

He can get such information as he thinks necessary.
I think, after all the Auditor General is a law unto himself.
I think, if I remember right, the government were not giving him that assistance that he ought to have to ascertain the cost of the bridge, and he took the law into his own hands.

There was a difference between the Department of Railways and the Auditor General, but I think I am correct in stating that in that case there was no difficulty in the Auditor General getting all the information that he wanted.

Was it not a fact that that department was quite willing to pay a bonus on the bridge at the exorbitant price that the company claimed it cost, and but for the fact that the Auditor General refused to pay and went into an inquiry himself, that bonus would have been paid and the consolidated revenue would have been that much worse off.
There was a difference of opinion between the Auditor General and the department, but 1 do not recall all the facts.

It is not a power that a public officer would abuse, at least we could not presume that he would abuse it. While it can do no harm, there might possibly be a case where it could do good to give him that power, which would be of benefit to the country. I think we gave some power to the Auditor General in the Act relating to the transcontinental railway, which was somewhat analogous to the power I am asking for now.

I have no doubt that if the Auditor General were to say that he wished to get access to the books of a company for the purpose of examining into a claim, the Minister of Railways, I think, would be bound to give him authority to do so ; I have no doubt he would. There has not been any difficulty of that kind that I know of. This provides that the Minister of Railways or any other person appointed by him may examine all the books. If the Auditor General were to say that in consequence of information he had he wished a person appointed to examine the books, I am sure that any Minister of Railways would authorize that person to represent him for that purpose. I do not think it needs any amendment.

I think I had incidentally brought to my notice during the present session, that the Auditor General did suggest something like that and that the minister, without mentioning who it was, took a very different view, and if it depended upon authorizing an examination of the books under such circumstances no examination would be made. It would be weil to make it clear that it was the duty of the Auditor General to make such a demand, and the duty of the minister to accede to the demand.

I am afraid I could not agree with my hon. friend as to the theory of the matter. I think responsibility in all these things is on the minister and not on the Auditor General. Theoretically I differ with my hon. friend ; but there is no practical difference, because no difficulty on that score has occurred. I do not think the Auditor General complains that he could not get information.
I think we all know he is pretty thorough in these things. So far as I am aware, he has always got all the information he desires.

I have had occasion to hold different views from the hon. gentleman as to what constitutes ministerial responsibility. Ministerial responsibility cannot go so far as to be of any advantage or security to the public in repairing harm after harm is done, or loss has occurred. I think I have stated before that ministerial responsibility does not always make restitution. The better way is to provide by statute against loss to the country through an officer whose duty it is to look after these things. To say that the minister is responsible is not enough. We might just as well say, and it would be carrying the argument to its legitimate conclusion, that each department over which a minister presides should take the responsibility therefor, and that there was no need of an auditor. A minister has a right to say, I am responsible for that, and I do not think an officer should interfere. I think, on the other hand, a safe anrl healthy course to take is to secure a scrutiny by an officer whose business it is to do that work.

Mr. Chairman, before you report these resolutions I want to remind the committee that in connection with one of the items for a subsidy in British Columbia an error occurred and that we have a separate resolution to add to the item. We have dealt with the matter and discussed it, but we must correct the error. In order to do that we will have to formally report these other resolutions ; I shall then ask the committee to sit again. This is in connection with the item for the Kootenay Central road.
Resolutions reported, read the first and second time and agreed to.

On motion of the Minister of Finance House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to provide as follows That the Governor in Council may, in addition to the mileage of railway proposed to he subsidized by item 66 of the resolutions respecting railway subsidies now 'before this House, grant a further subsidy to the Kootenay Central Railway Company, for the line of railway in the said item mentioned, not exceeding eighty miles, making the whole length not exceeding 186 miles, instead of 106 miles. (Correction of clerical error).
This is to correct the error to which attention has been called. As we have fully discussed the matter I move that this resolution be formally agreed to.

Resolution agreed to, reported, read the
first and second time, and agreed to.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 270) an Act to authorize the granting of subsidies in_aid of the construction of the lines of railway therein mentioned.

Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER informed the House that he had received a message from the Senate respecting amendments made by them to Bill (No. 21) an Act to consolidate and ameuu the laws respecting railways as follows
Tuesday, October 20, 1903. Resolved, that a message be sent to tlhe House of Commons by one of the Masters in Chancery, to inform that House, that the Senate doth accept the amendments made by the House of Commons to the Senate amendment No. 51 to Bill No. 21, intituled : ' An Act to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways,' and that the Senate doth not insist upon their amendments Nos. 6, 33, 45, 46 and 60 to the said Bill ; but doth insist upon their amendments Nos. 2,
3 and 4, for the reason that the clauses 5, 6 and 7 of the said Bill were an Interference with provincial and municipal rights which the Senate amendments minimized, while giving ait the same time jurisdiction to the board on all subject matters essential to the satisfactory working of the purposes set forth in the original sections 5, .6 and 7 of the said Bill,
The Senate doth also insist on its amendment No. 11, for the reason that in all tribunals there should be an appeal on points of law. It is equally in the interests of the individual and the company, especially when the appeal qan only be granted by leave of the board or of two judges of the Appellate Court.
The Senate doth insist upon its amendment No. 31, for the reason that the clause In its original form involves an interference with municipal rights.

The Senate doth also insist upon its amendment No. 40, for tlhe reason that cases may arise where the agreement was fair and just to the employee. The Senate suggests as an alternative to the words proposed to be inserted by the following amendment :-

The Senate doth also insist upon its amendment No. 70, for the reasons set forth in the objections to Nos. 2, 3 and 4.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved that:
A select committee composed of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Hon. Mr. Fielding, Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick and Hon. Mr. Blair, be appointed to draw up reasons to be offered at a conference with the Senate for disagreeing to certain amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 21) entitled an Act to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways.

I presume the desire of the government is to confine that committee to the members of the Privy Council in order that it may have the greater authority. I observe that all of the (members of the committee are members of the Privy Council except the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals.
He is a member of the Privy Council.
I would suggest the name of the hon. senior member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker).
There can be no objection to this.
I am not objecting.
It is quite unintentional that the hon. member (Mr. Barker) was omitted.
It is my mistake. I drew the resolution up hurriedly.
If the leader of the opposition would be willing to act, we would be pleased to have his assistance.
I would be glad if I could give any assistance. It may be that this being a government measure, it is the precedent that members of the government should represent members of the House.

It is not a controversial matter, and I will be glad if the House will allow me to move to add the names of the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker).
Motion, as amended, agreed to.

With regard to the dissent and the statement of the Canadian commissioners ?
